Chapter 5

The tensor glueball

5.1 Introduction

In chapters 2 and 3 we have discussed the scalar glueball, which is the lightest purely gluonic state. In fact,
there should exist a large spectrum of glueballs of various spin quantum numbers. This spectrum is one of
the earliest predictions of QCD and is intrinsically linked to its non-abelian gauge symmetry and confine-
ment [140]. Since then, various theoretical approaches have corroborated the existence of glueballs, see e.g.
[141, 142, 91, 143]. Among those approaches, Lattice QCD stands out, being able to compute, from first
principle, a large spectrum of glueball states [73, 72, 74, 144, 145, 146, 147] in a quenched approximation,
meaning that the quarks are non-dynamical. In [148] an unquenched calculation can be found. The glueball
spectrum gained from lattice QCD, in particular the one of [74], is also supported by a glueball resonance
gas model, similar to a hadron resonance gas model but with glueballs replacing the conventional hadrons,
which showed that the thermodynamic properties fit with what is known of pure Yang-Mills theory [149].
Recently, functional methods have also been successful at reproducing the glueball spectrum given by lattice
QCD, and could be a promising approach for calculating interactions and decays of glueballs [75, 150, 151],
which are difficult to calculate in lattice QCD.

While the different theoretical methods do not always give the same numerical outcomes, they generally
agree on several qualitative features. Namely, the lightest glueball state is a scalar (JPC = 0++), the
second-lightest is a tensor with JPC = 2++ (the tensor/scalar mass ratio can be an interesting quantity, see
e.g. [152]), and the third-lightest is a pseudoscalar (JPC = 0−+). For all the glueballs, their experimental
status is still inconclusive. However, for the lightest three states there do exist some notable candidates
[91]. Still, because glueballs will mix with regular mesons of the same quantum numbers and similar masses
and because of their poorly known decays, conclusive identification of glueballs in experiments is very difficult.

In this chapter, we concentrate on the tensor glueball. The tensor glueball is of interest to us for a number
of reasons. The first one, as we have mentioned before, is that it is the second lightest glueball state. The
second reason is the experimental observation of several isoscalar-tensor resonances which lie in the 2 GeV
region such as the f2(1430), f2(1565), f2(1640), f2(1810), f2(1910), f2(1950), f2(2010), f2(2150), and the
fJ(2220). One of these could be the tensor glueball, especially ones close to the lattice QCD predictions
of about 2 GeV. Attempts to find the tensor glueball in one of those f2 states has a long history, see e.g

66



CHAPTER 5. THE TENSOR GLUEBALL 67

[140, 153, 154, 155]. In particular, the fJ(2220) was historically considered as a good candidate for the tensor
glueball [156]. However in this chapter, our results will point towards the fJ(2220) not being a good tensor
glueball candidate anymore.
There have been various different lattice QCD simulations that have computed the physical mass of the tensor
glueball. Some of these predictions are: 2150(30)(100) MeV [144], 2324(42)(32) MeV [145], 2376(32) MeV [74],
2390(30)(120) MeV [73], and 2400(25)(120) MeV [72]. Furthermore, using QCD sum rules, the tensor glueball
mass has been found to be in the range of 2000-2300 MeV [76, 157]. The aforementioned functional method
gave a tensor glueball mass of around 2610 MeV [75]. Holographic QCD methods, based on the AdS/CFT cor-
respondence, have also been used to study glueballs for instance in [158, 78, 77, 159, 160, 161, 162, 163, 164].
The tensor glueball mass in these holographic calculations can be found anywhere from 1900 to 4300 MeV,
depending on the model and the values of the parameters [161, 163]. In general, while the numerical result
for the mass differs, different theoretical methods converge on the existence of a tensor glueball in the region
near 2000 MeV.
Some results are also known for the decays of the tensor glueball. For instance, in [77, 159], the decays
of the tensor glueball have been calculated in the Witten-Sakai-Sugimoto Model. It was found that if the
tensor glueball mass is above the threshold where it is able to decay into ρρ, the tensor glueball state is
quite broad. In other hadronic approaches such as [101, 165], decay ratios for the tensor glueball were also
found. However, these did not yet include an explicit realization of chiral symmetry, which we will do in this
chapter. The tensor glueball is also thought to be related to the occurrence of OZI suppressed process such
as π−p→ ϕϕn [166].
On the experimental side, a data analysis on decays of the J/ψ could be promising for the identification
of the scalar and tensor glueballs [140, 113, 167, 168]. The tensor glueball mass from this analysis would
be around 2210 MeV. Future experiments with measurable production of tensor glueballs are discussed in
[169, 170].
With all these in mind, it is then quite natural to ask what a chiral hadronic approach like the eLSM can tell
about us the tensor glueball state, especially in connection to its decays. This chapter deals exactly with this
question: we study the tensor glueball via a suitable extension of the eLSM used in the previous chapter. In
the past, other glueballs such as the scalar [171, 79], pseudoscalar [172, 173], and vector [98] glueballs have
been studied in the eLSM, which makes this a natural next step.
Within the eLSM framework, we will evaluate various decay rates. The most important will turn out to be
the ρρ/ππ decay ratio. We then compare the outcomes to the isoscalar-tensor states in the range close to
2000 MeV and find out that the resonance f2(1950) is, according to present data combined with the eLSM
predictions, our best candidate. We will also comment on the partial decay widths of the glueball and the
overall assignment of excited tensor states.

5.4.2 Classification of tensor meson states

The second point relates to the assignment of quark-antiquark tensor states. Up to now, we have considered
all isoscalar f2 states in the energy region about 2 GeV equally as potential tensor glueball candidates.
However, most of them should be interpreted as standard q̄q objects.
For this reason, it is useful look at how to classify them normally, rather than looking at their status as
a potential glueball. While the ground-state tensor mesons (with spectroscopic notation 13P2) are well
established as a2(1320), K∗2 (1430), f2(1270), and f ′2(1525), there is also a nonet of radially excited tensor
states (23P2) and a nonet of orbitally excited tensor states (13F2). Based on the quark model [100], the
orbitally excited tensor states are thought to be more massive than the radially excited tensor states, just
as with the excited vector mesons [116].
The nonet of radially excited tensor mesons consists of the following. The isotriplet state a2(1700), the
isodoublet states K∗2 (1980), and the isoscalar (mostly nonstrange) f2(1640). The mostly strange s̄s member



CHAPTER 5. THE TENSOR GLUEBALL 77

of the nonet could be assigned to f2(1910), or f2(1950), or f2(2010). The quark model review of the PDG
[2] considers f2(1950) as the radially excited s̄s state. However, the decay of that state does not quite fit
with the picture of a predominantly s̄s object. In particular, the experimental KK/ππ ratio is about 0.8
(see Table 5.4), while a s̄s state would imply a ratio larger than one. Furthermore, the mass is very close to
that of the tensor isodoublet member K∗2 (1980), which does not support it being a radially excited strange-
antistrange state.
For the state f2(1910), it is currently not clear if it corresponds to a separate resonance or if it is actually
the same as the f2(1950). It is therefore omitted from the PDG summary table. Its mass is even lighter
than K∗2 (1980), which makes it unlikely this state is an s̄s state. The decays also do not support it being
strange-antistrange. The decay mode ρρ should be suppressed, as well as a2(1320)π which should be smaller
than f2(1270)η. In the data (see Table 5.4), this is not the case.
On the other hand, the state f2(2010) is well established and is known to decay into ϕϕ and KK. This
makes it more likely be include strange contents, thus making it more suitable as the last radially excited
tensor meson.
Summarizing the discussion above, we might identify the nonet of radially excited tensor mesons as

{a2(1700), K∗2 (1980), f2(1640), f2(2010)} with 23P2 and JPC = 2++. (5.4.8)

With the f2(1910) being less well established, this leaves the f2(1950) as a potential glueball candidate. In
[184] it is also concluded that the f2(1950) does not fit the 33P2 nonet as the radial excitation of f2(1270),
and the mass is too low to otherwise fit in that nonet according to the Regge trajectory.

The situation for the orbitally excited states is not as clear. There are no well established isotriplet or isodou-
blet states that could be used to identify the nonet. Possible isoscalar resonances could be the f2(2150),
the f2(2300) or the f2(2340). The f2(2150) could correspond to a nonstrange isoscalar state belonging to
the next radially excited nonet 33P2, and the f2(2300) and the f2(2340) could be regarded as a single state,
which would be the s̄s state of this nonet. However, these resonances are all not well established, and more
information is needed to make a definitive statement on this nonet.

5.5 Conclusions

In this chapter, we expanded upon the previous chapter on tensor mesons and adapted it to the study of the
tensor glueball. We constructed chirally invariant Lagrangians which describe the tensor glueball decays.
From these we could find the decay ratios of certain channels for the tensor glueball. It turns out the
dominant decay channels involve two vector decay products. In particular, the channels ρρ and K∗K̄∗ are
large compared to the others.
From the large predicted ρρ/ππ ratio, it would follow that the tensor glueball itself is very broad, given the
estimate of the ππ mode being of the order of 10 MeV. furthermore, we also predict a very small decay width
of the tensor glueball into K∗(892)K. This specific decay mode could be useful to exclude potential glueball
candidates in the future.
Comparing the theoretical predictions to the experimental data shows that presently the best best match
between experimental data and eLSM predictions is for the f2(1950). This would also imply that the tensor
glueball is a relatively broad state. According to lattice QCD, the f2(1950) might be too light to be the

6.1 Introduction

The vector glueball’s mass is predicted to be in the range of 3.8 to 4 GeV based on lattice computations
[73, 74]. In contrast to the lightest glueball states, potential candidate states are lacking for the vector
glueball. However, it shares quantum numbers with the bound charmonium state J/ψ and its excited state,
the ψ(3686), which have quantum numbers in the spectroscopic notation n2S+1LJ as 13S1 for the J/ψ and
23S1 for the ψ(3686). These are believed to decay primarily through a 3-gluon channel, already making
their decays an interesting avenue in identifying glueballs experimentally. Furthermore, the vector glueball
in particular can play a role here, since it can (and in general will) mix with these states with the same
quantum numbers.

The J/ψ and ψ(3686) are nonrelativistic bound charm-anticharm states. Their primary decay is through
3 gluons, which in the nonrelativistic limit is proportional to the wave function at the origin. That is, the
decay width to some final state h consisting of light hadrons is [186, 187]

Γh = |ψ(r = 0)|2|M|2. (6.1.1)

Where ψ(r) is the position wavefunction of the system, and M is the matrix element associated with the
decay channel. This equation, albeit with different ψ(r) and M, holds for both the J/ψ and the ψ(3686).
One can then look at the ratio of their decay widths into a specific state. If one chooses to ignore phase
space factors –essentially ignoring the mass difference between the J/ψ and the ψ(3686) – only the unknown
ratio of wave functions remains. Computing these wave functions is no trivial task, but without knowledge
of the wave functions we can already see that the ratio of decay widths is almost independent of the final
state h into which it decays. The same argument holds for the decay into e+e−, for which this ratio is
experimentally well-known. Using PDG data on the e+e− channel we can compute this ratio:

relative to the 13% rule.

Experimentally, the first indication of the ρπ puzzle was observed in 1983 by the Mark II collaboration [188],
where the decay of the J/ψ into ρπ was substantial, but the decay width for the channel ψ(3686) → ρπ was
so small it was only observed decades later by CLEO and BES [189, 190]. Early on it was noticed that the
charmonium decays into ρπ break hadron helicity conservation [191] which follows from perturbative QCD
predictions. Understanding why this rule is broken may have important consequences for the applicability
of perturbative QCD to the decay of charmonium states or even other states at a similar mass.
There are many proposed explanations for the ρπ puzzle [192, 193]. A non-exhaustive list of explanations
not involving the vector glueball include

• Intrinsic charm components in the light mesons such as the ρ, which allow for new diagrams for the
decay of the J/ψ, which are suppressed for the ψ(3686) because the excited state is orthogonal to the
charm-anticharm component of the ρ [194].

• Suppression of the charm-anticharm wave function at the origin for a component of the ψ(3686) in
which the cc̄ is in a color-octet 3S1 state [195].

• Interference between 3-gluon and electromagnetic decays for the J/ψ decays, while the ψ(3686) decays
not through a 3-gluon, but through a specific configuration of 5 gluons [196].

• A large nonvalence gluon or quark-antiquark component present in the wavefunction of the ψ(3686),



CHAPTER 6. THE VECTOR GLUEBALL, MIXING, AND THE ρπ PUZZLE 81

which are not significant in the J/ψ since it is the lowest lying state. The valence and nonvalence
components then interfere destructively in the ρπ channel [197].

• Destructive interference between S-wave and D-wave components of the ψ(3686), which come from
mixing with the D-wave charmonium state ψ′′ [198].

• Final state interactions, which can be of similar order as tree level amplitudes. In particular, J/ψ → ρπ

would be enhanced by the a2ρ loop diagram, while for the ψ(3686) this can be canceled by the a1ρ
loop diagram [199].

• Cancellation between the amplitudes for the processes e+e− → ψ(3686) → ρπ and the direct decay
channel e+e− → ρπ [192].

Any such explanation tends to either postulate an enhancement for the decay J/ψ → ρπ, or a suppression
for the decay ψ(3686) → ρπ. The class of explanations we will treat here is that the ρπ puzzle is caused
by mixing with a vector glueball. In the past a mixing between the vector glueball with the J/ψ [200, 201],
as well as the ψ(3686) [202] have been considered. Given recent lattice predictions for the vector glueball
mass in the range of about 3.8 to 4 GeV [73, 74], the ψ(3686) is closer in mass to the vector glueball, and
so we will initially assume a mixing between the excited charmonium state and the vector glueball, but the
calculation can be easily adapted to have mixing between the J/ψ and the vector glueball instead. Aside
from the influence of the vector glueball, we will assume the 13% rule holds. This means that mixing of the
ψ(3686) with the vector glueball will fall into the category of suppression of the decay ψ(3686) → ρπ, and
mixing of the J/ψ with the vector glueball will be enhancement of the decay J/ψ → ρπ. We will use the
framework of the eLSM which we have introduced in Chapter 3 and applied in Chapters 4 and 5, as apply
a vector meson dominance (VMD) model, as before.

6.4 Conclusions

In this chapter we studied the decays of charmonium states, in particular in relation to the 13% rule and
its unexplained breaking, which is called the ρπ puzzle. This puzzle has been an open problem for over 40
years, and its solution could have implications in important aspects of charmonium physics. We attempted
to explain the ρπ puzzle via mixing of the ψ(3686) with the vector glueball. We have also introduced



CHAPTER 6. THE VECTOR GLUEBALL, MIXING, AND THE ρπ PUZZLE 87

electromagnetic decay channels through a vector meson dominance model, since these decay channels are
also expected to be relevant.
With three free parameters – the glueball coupling, the strong J/ψ coupling, and an energy scale – we
manage to make a reasonable description of the experimental data on the Qh ratio for the available V P
channels. The fit shows that, aside from the electromagnetic interactions, including the vector glueball and
its mixing with the ψ(3686) significantly improves the matching with experimental data. At the level of
this model, including the vector glueball mixing is necessary to satisfy the data. Even with electromagnetic
interactions playing a big role, they are by itself not enough. At this point the fit slightly prefers mixing of the
glueball with the ψ(3686), but we cannot definitively conclude on way or the other. The analysis can still be
expanded further; adding more decay channels, such as those where the 13% rule is not broken, is an obvious
extension. One could also include higher order diagrams for the strong interaction, and a different coupling
for mesons containing a strange quark as in [205]. Achieving a full description of the J/ψ and ψ(3686)

decays separately, rather than the ratio Qh, would also be a large improvement. One particularly promising
outcome of incorporating more decay channels and treating the ground state and excited charmonium decays
separately is that it might be possible to find a constraint on the mixing angle. This, in turn, can give us
an estimate on vector glueball decays, which can be used in an attempt to discover the vector glueball, or
used to compare with experiment in a similar manner as done in Chapter 5.



Chapter 7

Conclusion

In this thesis we have studied the spectroscopy and the decays of mesons of various types in models based
on effective Lagrangians, in particular the eLSM.
In chapter 2, we looked at a relatively simple model: a real scalar field coupled to a classical, time indepen-
dent source. It turns out that there is more to this model than initially meets the eye, and the historical
treatment of this model missed those aspects. Historically, the theory was approached as a limit of theories
with a time-dependent source, which turns off after some time, where the time when the interaction is turned
off is taken to infinity. The standard formalism of the S-matrix was then applied, which said it had to be
zero, and no scattering takes place. The main issue, as we have found by solving the model exactly, is
that the theory has a nonzero commutator between the Hamiltonian and momentum operator, so that the
asymptotically free in- and out-states necessary for the S-matrix formalism do not exist. Whether or not the
initial state is a particle number eigenstate or an energy state, which are distinct in the time independent
case, can no longer be distinguished in the time dependent case. Which of the two one ends up with then
depends on how the limit is taken. In short, the theory has no S-matrix. Hence, approaching the theory by
other theories that do have an S-matrix fails. By solving the theory exactly we have computed the decay of
the (particle) vacuum and its particle production over time, along with its large volume limits. The resulting
behavior is analogous to the Schwinger mechanism, and includes non-exponential decay, saturation at large
times, and an explicit realization of the quantum Zeno effect. This theory could potentially be a model for
a nonperturbative creation mechanisms of the a scalar particle in the presence of a medium. For example
the dilaton, which is seen as the scalar glueball, with a large amount within the f0(1710) according to the
eLSM, which then decays into detectable particles like pions, kaons, etc.

Afterwards, we turned to the extended Linear Sigma Model (eLSM) as the primary theoretical tool to
study the interactions of mesons. In Chapter 3 we have introduced the formalism of the eLSM, and in the
subsequent chapters we applied this.
In Chapter 4 we extended the eLSM to include the tensor and axial tensor spin 2 mesons. The axial tensor
mesons are poorly known at this point, while the tensor mesons are very well established. The match between
theory and experiment on the tensor mesons confirms their status as quark-antiquark objects. Using chiral
symmetry we use the tensor meson data to make predictions about the interactions of axial tensor mesons,
as well as make some predictions for yet unknown decay channels of the tensor mesons. We predict the axial
tensor meson masses, which lie around 300 to 400 MeV above the tensor meson masses, and their decays.

88



CHAPTER 7. CONCLUSION 89

The decay widths of the axial tensor mesons turn out to be very large in some channels. This explains why
they have not been successfully detected thus far, but also gives a specific direction in which to look for these
states.
In Chapter 5 we have included the tensor glueball in the eLSM, and studied its decays. Numerical predictions
for the decay widths cannot be made, but we can make estimates of the decay ratios. The dominant decay
channel is the decay into two vector mesons, in particular two ρ mesons. By comparing the structure of the
decay ratios to those of the plentiful candidate glueball resonances, we conclude that the f2(1950) is the best
candidate to be the tensor glueball, despite its large decay width.
In Chapter 6 we applied the eLSM to the decay of charmonium states. There is a long-standing open problem
with these states called the ρπ puzzle, which has to do with large breaking of the 13% rule established by
perturbative QCD. By incorporating electromagnetic decay channels and mixing with the vector glueball,
we drastically improve agreement with experimental values on the ratio of branching ratios, which break the
13% rule. While it does not explain the puzzle entirely, it is clear that including electromagnetic decays is an
important part of explaining the ρπ puzzle. It also shows that mixing with the vector glueball is potentially
a part of the explanation. More experimental data, which might falsify some of the explanations, and theo-
retical studies, that expand the model and data analysis, are necessary to achieve the full picture of this issue.

The results of this thesis could be interesting for ongoing experiments, such as CLAS, GlueX, and BE-
SIII, and for future ones, such as those taking place at the FAIR facility [206]. The model of Chapter 2 can
be used to model interactions of scalar mesons in the presence of a medium in heavy-ion collisions, and the
structure of the theory, where we do not have an S-matrix, can teach us about the structure of quantum field
theories. The results of Chapter 4 can aid in the discovery of the ground state axial tensor mesons. More
experimental data on the isoscalar tensor meson resonances around 2 GeV can lead to a better understanding
of the tensor glueball using the analysis of Chapter 5. In particular further studies on the f2(1950) could
tell us more about its status as the potential tensor glueball. The result of Chapter 6 can have implications
on the decay of charmonium states and the ρπ puzzle, but also on the decays of the vector glueball, which
so far has been elusive.

obvious, which is the number of colors Nc of the gauge group SU(Nc). This generalizes the QCD gauge group

titles.title: Phenomenology of Glueballs in Effective Hadronic Models

abstracts.value:
Motivated by the steady developments in gravitational-wave astronomy, this dis-
sertation focuses on the analytical aspects of black hole perturbation theory. We
present novel analytical techniques that deal with quasinormal modes (QNMs)
and scattering amplitudes of black holes.
Like a string or a bell, black holes tend to vibrate at the lowest possible frequency
or the fundamental frequency. These fundamental frequencies are known numer-
ically, but the analytic description or the mathematical tools necessary for their
understanding are not fully developed. In the first part of the dissertation, we
present one such tool, which utilizes the connection between equations describing
small perturbations of ordinary black holes and Seiberg-Witten theory.
In the next part, we investigate the vibrations of black holes embedded in four-
dimensional spacetime with negative or positive cosmological constant. In the
case of the negative cosmological constant, the Seiberg-Witten approach proves
to be more complicated to implement, and we propose an alternative method to set up perturbation theory for both small and large black holes in an analytical
manner. We reveal a new underlying recursive structure that involves multiple
polylogarithms.
In the final part of the dissertation, we introduce a novel approach to black
hole scattering amplitudes based on a new set of special functions called multiple
polyexponential integrals. By solving the Regge-Wheeler equation perturbatively
in the small-frequency regime, we determine the monodromy in the near-spatial
infinity region and derive a specific partial diﬀerential equation on the elements
of the scattering matrix. As a result, we pinpoint the exact form of scattering
amplitudes in Schwarzschild spacetime.

titles.title: New Analytic Methods in Black Hole Perturbation Theory

abstracts.value:
In this thesis, we develop and apply methods inspired by two-dimensional conformal field
theory, supersymmetric gauge theory, and topological string theory to the study of spectral
problems. In the first part, we investigate periodic spectral problems governed by the
Lamé and Heun equations, including confluent limits of the latter. These equations arise
both as classical limits of BPZ equations satisfied by degenerate Virasoro conformal blocks
and as quantized Seiberg–Witten curves of four-dimensional N = 2 SU(2) gauge theories.
The two descriptions are related by the AGT correspondence, under which degenerate
classical conformal blocks are mapped to surface-defect partition functions in the Nekrasov–
Shatashvili (NS) limit. We solve the connection problem for the Lamé equation and develop
a systematic resummation procedure, based on suitable limits of blow-up equations, for bulk
and defect NS functions. The resummation resolves their singular instanton expansions at
resonant values of the Floquet exponent and reveals the branch structure of the accessory
parameters and Floquet solutions, whose branch points determine the edges of spectral
bands and gaps. For the Lamé equation, the resonant limit of the resummed accessory
parameter agrees with the values obtained independently from isomonodromic and orbifolddefect
constructions. The latter also provides the corresponding (anti-)periodic solutions.
For the Heun equation, we extend the resummation procedure to include the Floquet
solutions, obtaining at resonance both the accessory parameters and the corresponding
(anti-)periodic solutions. We further construct their logarithmic companions and analyze
the resonant monodromy, distinguishing the mass loci where spectral gaps close from the
smaller loci where the resonant monodromy becomes semisimple.
In the second part, we study finite-difference equations obtained by quantizing the mirror
curves of the Y N,0 geometries, which engineer five-dimensional N = 1 SU(N) gauge theories.
In the framework of the open topological string/spectral theory (TS/ST) correspondence,
we construct exact generalized eigenfunctions that are expected to be entire in the open
and closed moduli and to become square-integrable when the spectral moduli belong
to the appropriate exact quantization locus. Their four-dimensional limit gives explicit
analytic solutions to the eigenvalue problem associated with HN = 2ΛN cosh(p) + VN(x),
where VN(x) is an arbitrary monic polynomial of degree N. These operators are solvable
finite-difference deformations of the Schrödinger Hamiltonians p2+VN(x), and our solutions
describe both bound states and resonances. We also identify special loci at which the
eigenfunctions exhibit enhanced decay. For confining potentials, this enhancement leads
to spectral degeneracies, while for potentials unbounded from below, it produces squareintegrable
states with real energies. We finally discuss the related operators with a sinh(p)
kinetic term, an inverted potential −VN(x), or both.

Abstract

Despite the significant advancements in quantum field theory and general relativity, the two
fields have developed mostly in parallel. A theory describing both gravitational and quantum
effects up to high energies, namely a theory of quantum gravity, has yet to be established.
Although string theory has been one of the most promising candidates for such a theory, it
produces an enormous number of candidate low-energy effective field theories. To identify
which of these, or other, effective field theories are compatible with quantum gravity, a suitable
set of criteria is required. Such consistency conditions are formulated within the swampland
program in the form of swampland conjectures. This is a framework aiming to separate the
theories admitting an ultraviolet completion from the swampland, the theories that do not.
These criteria are often motivated by string theory but they also provide a fresh perspective on
string-theoretic results.

This thesis studies a particular swampland conjecture, the Emergence Proposal. This proposal
claims that the low-energy effective action can be understood as a quantum effect, more precisely
by an integrating-out procedure of light states in asymptotic limits of the moduli space. We
will present a concrete refinement of this idea realized in a particular M-theory limit, where
only the M-theory circle will grow large, with other compact directions remaining of fixed
size in eleven-dimensional units. M-theory is considered to be the eleven-dimensional theory
unifying the known string theories. However, due to its strongly coupled nature, many aspects
of its quantum structure remain unknown. We will present evidence supporting this proposal,
based on supersymmetrically protected gravitational and gauge couplings in Calabi-Yau and
toroidal compactifications, described mainly by automorphic forms admitting Schwinger-like
integral representations. Specifically, we consider the prepotential of the resolved conifold,
the R4-term in dimensions down to four, and the F 4 gauge coupling in six dimensions. It
will become evident that our refinement is closely related to their mathematical structure in a
highly non-trivial way. This connection becomes manifest through the implementation of an
appropriate regularization procedure for the amplitudes under consideration, including minimal
subtraction and analytic continuation, and the interpretation of the theory’s ultraviolet cutoff,
the eleven-dimensional Planck scale, in a manner analogous to the role of the string scale in
string perturbation theory. Concretely, it will be interpreted as the energy scale distinguishing
perturbative from non-perturbative degrees of freedom, rather than a hard cutoff. As a result,
the complete particle towers whose typical mass scale is not above this cutoff will be integrated
out. These are Kaluza-Klein modes and particles obtained from branes wrapped transversally to
the large M-theory circle. We will further contemplate how our results may be used to extract
information about this poorly understood corner of string theory.





Zusammenfassung

Trotz der bedeutenden Fortschritte in der Quantenfeldtheorie und der Allgemeinen Relativ-
itätstheorie haben sich beide Forschungsgebiete weitgehend parallel entwickelt. Eine Theorie,
die sowohl gravitative als auch quantenmechanische Effekte bis hin zu hohen Energien kon-
sistent beschreibt – eine Theorie der Quantengravitation – steht bislang noch aus. Obwohl
die Stringtheorie zu den vielversprechendsten Kandidaten für eine solche Theorie zählt, führt
sie zu einer enormen Zahl möglicher effektiver Feldtheorien bei niedrigen Energien. Um zu
bestimmen, welche dieser oder anderer effektiver Feldtheorien mit einer konsistenten Theorie
der Quantengravitation vereinbar sind, bedarf es geeigneter Konsistenzkriterien. Solche Bedin-
gungen werden im Rahmen des Swampland-Programms in Form von Swampland-Vermutungen
formuliert. Ziel dieses Programms ist es, diejenigen Theorien, die eine konsistente ultravio-
lette Vervollständigung zulassen, von denjenigen des Swamplands abzugrenzen, für die dies
nicht möglich ist. Die Vermutungen werden häufig durch Erkenntnisse aus der Stringtheorie
motiviert, eröffnen zugleich jedoch neue Perspektiven auf stringtheoretische Resultate.

In dieser Arbeit untersuchen wir eine spezielle Swampland-Vermutung, das sogenannte Emer-
gence Proposal. Diese besagt, dass sich die effektive Niederenergie-Wirkung als ein quan-
tenmechanischer Effekt verstehen lässt, genauer als das Resultat des Ausintegrierens leichter
Zustände. Wir stellen eine konkrete Verfeinerung dieser Idee vor, die in einem bestimmten
M-Theorie-Limes realisiert wird, in dem ausschließlich der M-Theorie-Kreis groß wird, während
alle übrigen kompakten Richtungen in elfdimensionalen Einheiten eine feste Größe behalten.
Die M-Theorie wird als die elfdimensionale Theorie angesehen, die die bekannten Stringthe-
orien vereinigt. Aufgrund ihrer stark gekoppelten Natur bleiben jedoch viele Aspekte ihrer
Quantenstruktur bislang unverstanden. Wir liefern Evidenz für diesen Vorschlag anhand su-
persymmetrisch geschützter Gravitations- und Eichkopplungen in Calabi-Yau- und toroidalen
Kompaktifizierungen, die im Wesentlichen durch automorphe Formen beschrieben werden
und Schwinger-artige Integraldarstellungen besitzen. Konkret betrachten wir das Präpoten-
tial der aufgelösten Konifold, den R4-Term bis einschließlich vier Dimensionen sowie die F 4

-Eichkopplung in sechs Dimensionen. Dabei zeigt sich, dass unsere Verfeinerung in hochgradig
nichttrivialer Weise mit deren mathematischer Struktur verknüpft ist. Dieser Zusammenhang
wird durch die Einführung eines geeigneten Regularisierungsverfahrens für die betrachteten
Amplituden sichtbar, das Minimalsubtraktion und analytische Fortsetzung umfasst, sowie
durch eine Interpretation des ultravioletten Cutoffs der Theorie, der elfdimensionalen Planck-
skala, in Analogie zur Rolle der Stringskala in der Stringstörungstheorie. Konkret wird dieser
nicht als harter Cutoff verstanden, sondern als die Energieskala interpretiert, welche pertur-
bative von nicht-perturbativen Freiheitsgraden trennt. Daraus folgt, dass die vollständigen
Teilchentürme ausintegriert werden, deren charakteristische Massenskala diese Energieskala
nicht überschreitet. Dabei handelt es sich um Kaluza-Klein-Moden sowie um Teilchen, die
aus Branen hervorgehen, welche auf Zyklen zum großen M-Theorie-Kreis gewickelt sind.
Abschließend diskutieren wir, wie sich unsere Ergebnisse nutzen lassen, um neue Erkenntnisse
über diesen bislang nur unzureichend verstandenen Bereich der Stringtheorie zu gewinnen.

Introduction

Curiosity and pattern recognition are human instincts essential for survival. At the same time,
they are the driving forces of physics, theoretical physics in particular. Using the language of
mathematics and often initiating developments in many areas thereof, theoretical physicists
aspire to discover the underlying connections between physical phenomena, often manifesting
in completely different setups or energy scales. The success of these efforts does not only serve
the purpose of interpreting a physical model in a more fundamental manner, but also often
provides the appropriate framework to discover new phenomena.

This quest has been particularly fruitful in the past couple of centuries. We have progressed
from Newtonian mechanics to quantum mechanics [1], allowing us to describe microscopic
systems. The desire to reconcile mechanics with electromagnetism paved the way for special
relativity [2]. Let us appreciate these breakthroughs on a conceptual level. Humanity learned
that it cannot rely on its physical senses alone, as not all effects have an obvious classical
analogue. Wave-particle duality, quantum superposition and the unification of space and time
are only a few instances where these theories invite us to expand our intuition beyond what the
naked eye captures. These two physical frameworks were later brought together in quantum
field theory [3]. This remains to this day one of the most successful frameworks developed,
with the standard model of particle physics being arguably its greatest achievement. The
standard model provides a unified description of electroweak and strong interactions. The
particle content it predicts has been confirmed experimentally, with the last piece of the puzzle
being the Higgs boson, discovered in 2012 at the LHC at CERN [4], almost 50 years after its
prediction [5].

There is, however, a fundamental interaction missing from this picture, gravity. Another
breakthrough of the previous century was the formulation of general relativity [6]. This
sparked a major conceptual advancement in the way spacetime is viewed. Rather than being
treated as a fixed background which simply hosts other interactions, it is now promoted to a
dynamical field. Spacetime geometry is understood as a dynamical entity, with the curvature
being related to the theory’s energy momentum tensor via Einstein’s equations. This provided
the framework in which black holes and gravitational waves arise naturally as solutions of
Einstein’s equations [7]. The latter were detected almost a century later by LIGO and VIRGO
[8]. The consideration of dynamical solutions paved the way for modern cosmology and the
Big Bang model, which is the modern interpretation of ideas laid out soon after the birth of
general relativity [9]. However, general relativity is a classical theory, valid at sufficiently low
energies and small curvatures.

One might optimistically hope that the next step would be to simply quantize general relativity
and embed it in the standard model. This was, of course, attempted, but faced a serious
hurdle, the non-renormalizability of the theory [10, 11]. This implies that perturbative general



2 Introduction

relativity is not ultraviolet-complete as a quantum field theory since divergences cannot be
cured by a finite number of (counter-)terms. One can quantify the energy at which perturbative
general relativity is expected to break down via the Planck scale MPl ≃ 1.22× 1019GeV. This
shortcoming implies that one must either abandon any hope for describing all forces in a single
model, or resort to completely different methods.

Working with general relativity as an ultraviolet-incomplete framework has itself been quite
fruitful. In semi-classical gravity [12], gravity is treated classically, while allowing for in-
teractions with quantum matter systems. This is particularly convenient for cosmological
applications. This framework also laid the foundations of yet another important conceptual
advancement, namely that black hole systems can be understood as thermodynamic objects.
The entropy/area law of Bekenstein-Hawking [13, 14] quantifies this, while already providing
an instance where a possible interpretation of a phenomenon demands a quantum theory of
gravity. For the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy to admit a statistical interpretation in terms of
microscopic states, these states and their relation to the macroscopic gravitational description
should ultimately be understood within a theory of quantum gravity. Such a theory would also
be required to understand the evaporation of black holes [14]. Further examples of problems
that would require a theory of quantum gravity are the understanding of the early universe and
the treatment of singularities, while the hope is that such a theory could also provide insights
into hierarchy problems, for example by justifying the observed tiny value of our universe’s
cosmological constant [15]. A theory of quantum gravity can in turn potentially be related to
understanding the structure of dark matter, as our standard description in terms of the ΛCDM
model, which is so far our most successful fit with cosmological observations (see [16]) also
relies on semi-classical approximations.

Having estimated how far semi-classical approximations of general relativity can take us, we
must face the question of how to look for a theory of quantum gravity. One can insist on
assuming that classical Einstein gravity provides the required dynamical degrees of freedom,
but what needs to be modified is the employed quantization procedure. Notable examples of
such approaches are asymptotic safety [17], canonical quantum gravity [18] and its modern
development, loop quantum gravity [19], spin foam models [20], dynamical triangulations [21]
and others. While these feature novel conceptual viewpoints and sophisticated mathematical
tools, unification of forces and description of black holes remain generally challenging for them.
These difficulties provide further motivation for considering an alternative route, which is to
reconsider what the fundamental degrees of freedom are. Although this might seem radical
given the success of quantum field theories and general relativity, the evolution of quantum
mechanics has already taught us that when probing different energy scales the fundamental
degrees of freedom can vary drastically e.g. from a table to a molecule, an atom and eventually
quarks.

String theory to the rescue?

Postulating that the fundamental degrees of freedom in nature are not pointlike, but one-
dimensional, gives rise to string theory. Although initially introduced as a candidate theory of
hadrons [22], string theory is arguably the leading candidate for a quantum theory of gravity.



Introduction 3

It naturally contains a massless spin-two excitation identified with the graviton and can accom-
modate both gravitational and gauge interactions within a common framework. Thanks to the
extended nature of its fundamental constituents, it softens ultraviolet divergences of amplitudes
and opens the way for understanding theories possessing (certain) singularities. Importantly, it
provides a microscopic picture for black hole physics, reproducing the Bekenstein-Hawking
entropy formula [23]. In fact, this is only one instance of the holographic principle [24], the
notion that all the information of a quantum system is encoded in the surface of the region it
occupies. String theory has also provided the framework for perhaps one of the most concrete
realizations of this idea, which is the correspondence between a gravitational theory on an
anti-de Sitter spacetime and a gauge theory/conformal field theory on its boundary, known as
the AdS/CFT correspondence [25]. Remarkably, this is one of the few instances where we can
achieve strong-weak coupling duality, namely we can relate a weakly coupled, perturbative
string theory to a strongly coupled field theory. We cannot resist commenting on the technical
beauty of string theory, which relates physical amplitudes to topics of pure mathematics, such
as topology. String theory, viewed simply as a perturbative ultraviolet-complete quantum
framework for gravity, deserves study, at the very least as a theoretical testing ground for what
the consistency conditions for such a theory might be.

Admittedly, string theory nevertheless poses several conceptual and phenomenological chal-
lenges. For instance, it is much better understood in supersymmetric cases and its consistent
quantization naturally takes place in ten dimensions, not in the four dimensions we believe to
be living in. The fact that to this day supersymmetry has not been observed up to the energies
reachable by current collider experiments motivates further studies of non-supersymmetric
string theories, or setups where at least at the very end of the model-building procedure, super-
symmetry is broken. Both of these options are challenging but not impossible. The notion of
extra dimensions notably predates string theory and dates back to the work of Kaluza [26], who
suggested that “one make the otherwise extremely odd decision to ask for help from a new fifth
dimension of the world" to attempt to describe gauge theories and gravity in a unified manner.
The way string theory deals with these additional dimensions is by compactifying them, at
the cost of introducing (typically many) additional light fields. This is closely related to the
fact that the landscape of string vacua has been known to be extremely large, with estimates
ranging from 10500 [27] to even 10272000 [28]. Imposing restrictions on the allowed particle
content can reduce such numbers, with minimally supersymmetric standard models estimated
at a billion [29] and models with the exact chiral spectrum of the standard model estimated at
a quadrillion [30].

What separates the Landscape from the Swamp?

How does one navigate through such a vast landscape of models? Understanding this question
has given rise to a whole research field within string phenomenology, the swampland program.
The central goal of this program is to characterize which effective field theories admit an
ultraviolet completion within a theory of quantum gravity. Although the topic is motivated
primarily by considering string compactifications and how to identify which string-theoretic
effective theories, despite appearing to be consistent as quantum field theories, cannot be
considered as low-energy limits of quantum gravity, it also collects evidence from other areas of



4 Introduction

physics, such as black hole physics. The program thus aspires to identify universal consistency
conditions. The effective field theories satisfying such consistency conditions form the so-
called landscape, while the rest populate the swampland. Of course, as the name of the
program suggests, it is easier to exclude theories than to directly pinpoint the complete set
of consistency requirements imposed by quantum gravity. This might seem pessimistic, but
given the complexity of the problem, we will content ourselves with any available evidence
for quantum gravity theories. After all, “you cannot argue with a tiger with your head in its
mouth"1.

A fundamental underlying principle of quantum gravity that is utilized in the swampland
program is the notion of mixing between ultraviolet and infrared physics. This may be consid-
ered counterintuitive, since we are used to considering effective theories valid at a particular
energy range as not requiring input from energies outside this regime. However, due to non-
renormalizability we cannot expect gravity to reveal its secrets in an order-by-order manner, so
this feature provides a compelling alternative. To be more concrete, we have already encoun-
tered a manifestation of ultraviolet/infrared mixing in the form of the Bekenstein-Hawking
formula, relating a macroscopic quantity (area) to a microscopic one (entropy). In this thesis, we
will encounter other variations of this notion, for example in the form of the theory’s ultraviolet
cutoff being determined by its light-state spectrum.

The swampland program is built on a set of postulated consistency criteria on effective field
theories, the swampland conjectures, the first one being formulated in 2006 [31]. In the 20
years after the first conjecture, the program has given birth to numerous further consistency
requirements, most of which are interrelated, thus forming a large web. As a general property,
these typically focus on extreme values of the field space, addressing the proper treatment
of the theory there or even the appearance of certain, possibly new, degrees of freedom.
These statements have been extensively checked in the context of string compactifications and
compared e.g. with black hole arguments. At the same time, considerable efforts have been put
into utilizing them to establish connections with our observed universe and ideally even offer
experimentally testable predictions. One of the most attractive such avenues has been the Dark
Dimension Scenario [32], predicting the existence of a compact direction at the order of the
micron scale. In fact, its size is intriguingly related to the size of the universe’s vacuum energy
and believed to be testable within the next decades.

Can M-theory emerge from the Swamp?

Swampland principles have also served as guiding principles for revisiting string-theoretic
considerations from a modern viewpoint. This will also be at the core of the present thesis. In
fact, we will present evidence about why a particular swampland statement, the Emergence
Proposal [33], seems to admit its strongest realization in a particular corner of the string theory
framework, which to this day is arguably one of the least understood ones, M-theory.

In ten dimensions, one encounters five different supersymmetric string theories, which could
naturally give rise to the question: are they all on equal footing? Analogously to how Kaluza

although no reliable primary source is known.



Introduction 5

turned for help to an additional dimension, a similar idea was proposed by Witten, initiating
the second superstring revolution by suggesting that there exists an eleven-dimensional theory
underlying all of them, M-theory [34]. Using M-theory, all the known superstring theories
could be related to each other by dualities, a powerful tool often employed in string theory.
To this day, very little is known about M-theory. This is due to the fact that it is still typically
understood as a strongly coupled limit of string theory, containing higher-dimensional objects,
which, unlike strings, have not yet been quantized in a fashion appropriate for the formulation
of a perturbative theory.

Emergence is a very general concept, admitting different interpretations across different areas of
research ranging from linguistics to physics, with the common underlying principle being that
it refers to properties of a system that do not appear on the level of its individual components.
In the context of quantum gravity it has been defined [35] as the appearance of properties of a
system that are novel with respect to other (more fundamental) descriptions of the same system
and robust in the sense of characterizability and reproducibility. This definition resonates
with our discussion so far about how the identification of the fundamental degrees of freedom
can change depending on the energy scale or the phenomenon under consideration. In the
context of the swampland program, a similar notion has appeared, in which the way one
distinguishes between fundamental and non-fundamental degrees of freedom can be made
concrete. The Emergence Proposal studies how terms in an effective theory can be understood
as quantum effects, derived by integrating out certain degrees of freedom. In the present thesis,
we will provide examples showcasing how such a procedure can give rise to complete results
for both gravitational and gauge couplings, specifically when approaching M-theory. A key
point in achieving this has been identifying which direction in parameter space is the most
convenient one for such an analysis and what is the appropriate spectrum of particle states to
be integrated out. These states then act as the fundamental particle-like degrees of freedom
for (compactified) M-theory with all other states acting as non-perturbative objects. We will
review how this particular subset of states is compatible with the mathematical structure of
the related amplitudes and with the expected properties of a quantized M-theory. This analysis
sheds fresh light on a challenging topic, with very limited input in the past 30 years.

Thesis Outline

Let us summarize the structure of the present thesis. In the first part, we will begin with a
short (and admittedly biased by the author’s interests) review of basic aspects of string theory
in chapter 1. The goal will be to clarify notions and features already mentioned and make the
content of the thesis to some extent self-contained. The expert reader may safely proceed to
chapter 2, where some aspects of the swampland program and recent developments therein
will be presented.

1.1.1 String Perturbation Theory

We have so far considered how to generalize the action of a free point particle to that of a string,
but how would we introduce interactions? In quantum field theories, one typically works at the
level of a perturbative expansion, namely identifies a small expansion parameter and organizes
the various contributions to physical observables in powers of this parameter. A crucial element
to achieve this is the consideration of scattering amplitudes, which can be understood as sums
over Feynman diagrams. To consider higher-order terms in the perturbative expansion one
typically considers diagrams with increasing numbers of loops.

The notion of a Feynman diagram admits a natural generalization to closed strings. This can
already be understood at the level of the bosonic string. Rather than considering incoming and
outgoing lines, one considers incoming and outgoing strings, whose interactions are described
by splitting and joining processes, namely by the topology of the corresponding worldsheet (see
e.g. Figure 1.2). A scattering amplitude would then correspond to a summation over worldsheets
of inequivalent topologies. One way to motivate this is to reconsider the symmetries of (1.2).
These symmetries allow the addition of a topological term, namely

1.1.2 One-Loop Partition Function and Modular Invariance

Partition functions appear naturally in path integral approaches to quantum field theory as
generating functionals for n-point functions. They are also encountered in statistical mechanics,
where they can be thought of as a sum over all possible configurations weighted by the
factor e−βH , where β = 1/kBT is the Boltzmann factor, kB is the Boltzmann constant and
H is the Hamiltonian, the generator of time translations. In fact, the two approaches can
straightforwardly be related by considering a Euclidean quantum field theory with the time
direction compactified on a circle of radius R ≃ β. From a mathematical perspective, partition
functions can be viewed as weighted sums of characters of representations of the symmetry
algebra.

The simplest example of a partition function in string theory appears in the context of the
closed bosonic string. As discussed, its worldsheet has the topology of a cylinder. A toroidal
worldsheet can be constructed by gluing together the ends of that cylinder, after first potentially
performing a twist. According to our previous discussion, a toroidal worldsheet corresponds to
one-loop effects.

string theory, at least if one wishes to make contact with our (apparently) four-dimensional
physical world, we pause our presentation of ten-dimensional string theories here to address
the issue of compactification.

As mentioned in the introduction, independently of string theory the idea of compactifying
additional dimensions was already proposed by T. Kaluza [26] and further developed by O.
Klein [50] with the aim to provide a unified description of gravity and electromagnetism. The
prototypical example of Kaluza-Klein reduction on a circle is reviewed in Appendix B, as it can
already motivate the notion of a modulus field.

Orbifolds are among the simplest generalizations of manifolds that include singularities. In
short, we can say that they are topological spaces locally modeled on quotients of manifolds by a
finite group G, which potentially has non-trivial fixed points, which, if present, will correspond
to singularities. Therefore, it is not surprising that they can be singular limits of smooth
manifolds, but one can also recover those manifolds from the orbifolds via a mathematical
procedure which is described as blowing-up the singularities. We summarize this process in
the context of the K3 manifold and how it can be understood from the point of view of a T 4/Z2

orbifold in Appendix A.3. This definition can be compared with the quotient definition of the
torus we gave earlier, for which there exist no fixed points and therefore no singularities. One
can, however, construct toroidal orbifolds by further quotients. The easiest such example is a
particularly simple geometry, S1/Z2.

Consider a free bosonic string compactified on S1 and a Z2 symmetry acting on it as

I1 : X(τ, σ)→ −X(τ, σ) . (1.53)

1.3 Dualities

At this stage, we are familiar with the fundamental aspects of the five ten-dimensional super-
string theories, but a natural question is whether these theories are completely inequivalent.
This brings us to one of the most beautiful aspects of string theory, dualities. In contrast to
e.g. gauge theories, in string theory dualities can link not only different regimes of a coupling,
but even seemingly distinct theories on different spacetime geometries. We will now present
some fundamental dualities in string theory, providing some examples of how they lead to
dualities in string compactifications.

1.3.1 Open-Closed Duality

The concept of dualities appears already at the level of the fundamental objects of the theory,
the open and closed strings. A first manifestation of duality arises in the relation between the
open- and closed-string channels. An open-string loop amplitude is equivalent to a tree-level
closed string exchange amplitude. This is commonly referred to as open-closed duality.

Recall how we defined the one-loop partition function of a closed bosonic string by gluing the
ends of its worldsheet to create the topology of a torus, namely by introducing a periodicity
in the “time" coordinate τ . Introducing a time periodicity in the open string implies that its
worldsheet becomes a cylinder. This is exactly the topology of a closed string worldsheet, but
with the roles of τ and σ interchanged. The same amplitude can therefore be interpreted either
as a one-loop open-string amplitude or as a tree-level closed-string exchange. Note that this is
a precise equality. Importantly for our later applications, this is an instance of string theory
reinterpreting classical effects as quantum effects.

Dp-branes have at this point been defined solely in terms of open strings, but it turns out
that they also fit nicely into this picture. The boundary conditions via which they are defined
from an open string perspective can be reinterpreted as a boundary state in the closed string
Hilbert space. In fact, the boundary states are coherent states, which can be understood as
emitting and absorbing closed strings (see also Figure 1.7). This picture has a nice analogy with
the gauge-gravity correspondence, as we have seen that the closed string sector includes the
gravitational sector and Dp-branes host gauge theories.

each other. In this case, it is applied not only to compactification radii but also to the gauge
lattice and Wilson lines. The inclusion of the latter is necessary due to the different gauge
groups of the two heterotic theories.

However, note that the quantization of strings does not imply that quantizing any extended
object and organizing an appropriate perturbative expansion is straightforward. Unlike the
string worldsheet action, a Polyakov-type membrane worldvolume action does not possess
a Weyl symmetry and therefore membranes cannot be described by a (free) conformal field
theory. Although several steps have been made in understanding the quantization of the
simplest extended objects of M-theory, the supermembranes, a complete perturbative quantum
theory is not available at present.

Let us briefly review some of the subtleties related to their quantization. When performing
gauge fixing, which in the string case corresponded to picking the conformal gauge and working
with a two-dimensional free conformal field theory, one finds a three-dimensional interacting
theory, complicating quantization strategies. Additionally, organizing a genus expansion on the
topological level seems far from trivial, as a closed 3-dimensional manifold has vanishing Euler
characteristic. It seems that supermembranes are also challenging the idea of first quantization,
as they have a continuous excitation spectrum. A membrane can develop very long and thin
spikes, “tubes", which can grow arbitrarily long without costing energy.12 These can connect
various membranes, so that generally one cannot consider a conserved membrane number.
Equivalently, one is directly working with an analogue of a second quantized state. For a
pedagogical review of these issues see e.g. [70], although we will also return to some of them
in the next section in order to exhibit how these issues are addressed to a certain extent by
matrix models.

As of this day, a quantization of the supermembrane in a fashion appropriate for setting up a
perturbative theory has not been achieved. Since we thus typically only directly understand
M-theory as the strong coupling limit of type IIA or E8 ×E8 heterotic theory, one could argue
that this is not necessarily an underlying theory but an additional point in the duality star, with
the underlying theory of quantum gravity still not having been identified (see Figure 1.10). For
completeness, let us point out that recently progress has been made in better understanding
how such a web of dualities could be formed for non-supersymmetric string theories and
M-theory [71–75].

1.5.1 BFSS Conjecture

The difficulty of formulating a perturbative quantum theory of supermembranes naturally leads
to considering whether alternative objects could be used as fundamental degrees of freedom.
We will now review what has perhaps been the most fruitful related approach, relying on
matrix models. As the name suggests, these are theories whose fundamental degrees of freedom
are matrices rather than fields defined on a spacetime manifold. Interestingly, in such a setup
geometry and locality are not fundamental inputs, but are expected to arise dynamically. In
this section, we review a matrix model whose properties have motivated the refinement of
the swampland conjecture that constitutes the central topic of this thesis. At the same time, it
illustrates the challenges involved in formulating M-theory, thereby further highlighting the
significance of our results for M-theory compactifications.

Despite the great interest the BFSS matrix model has received in the past three decades, many
pieces of the puzzle are still missing. Its structure makes computations of scattering amplitudes
technically involved and the limit in which it is defined is not directly related to the standard

this framework both dynamical and gravitational effects appear to be of quantum nature is a
very attractive feature for a candidate quantum gravity theory. BFSS has also been related to
holography since the strongly-coupled large-N regime of the D0-brane quantum mechanics is
conjectured to be dual to the near-horizon black D0-brane geometry in type IIA supergravity
and has been used in related numerical tests [87]. For a more recent study on the relation
between BFSS and holography see e.g. [88].

Matrix models need not be considered only in the context of M-theory. Notable examples are the
Ishibashi-Kawai-Kitazawa-Tsuchiya (IKKT) model for type IIB [89, 90], the Itoyama–Tsuchiya
model for type I [91] and matrix string theory for type IIA [92–94].

Chapter 2

Swampland Program and Emergence

This chapter aims to provide a focused review of the swampland program, with particular
emphasis on its aspects relevant for the present thesis. The interested reader can obtain a
broader overview, for example through the following reviews and notes [33, 95–99].

2.1 Overview

At this point, we have reviewed some fundamental aspects of string theory and M-theory. In
doing so, we have already encountered the supergravity actions used as low-energy descriptions
of string theory. What we have not yet done is discuss to what extent these are compatible
with general expectations of effective field theories. On a fundamental level, properties such as
unitarity seem reasonable both from a string theory and an effective field theory perspective,
while modular invariance, for instance, has no obvious analog within ordinary effective field
theory. On the string theory side, a principle or mechanism capable of distinguishing among
the vast number of background solutions for string theory, corresponding to different choices
of background fields and fluxes, is needed. The swampland program aims to address the
complementary issue of whether quantum gravity considerations render seemingly consistent
effective field theories incompatible with an ultraviolet completion.

The central idea of the swampland program [100] is that only a subset of the effective field
theories that appear consistent, for example, by satisfying requirements such as the absence of
anomalies and unitarity, can admit an ultraviolet completion within a theory of quantum gravity.
This subset is called the (quantum gravity) landscape, while the rest form the swampland. A
schematic depiction of this idea is presented in Figure 2.1. Importantly, especially after the
development of the swampland program, it is expected that within the vast space of candidate
effective theories derived from string theory, those forming the space of low-energy effective
theories of quantum gravity occupy only a very tiny portion. To quantify this intuition, recall
that, as reviewed in the introduction, for models derived from type IIB string theory, estimates
as large as 10500 [27] have been made for the number of solutions. Such estimates not only
highlight the necessity of organizing principles within the space of string theory solutions, but
also foreshadow the difficulty in formulating such principles.

The expectation that not every effective theory can be utilized as a low-energy description of
quantum gravity is perhaps natural, but raises the question: how can we distinguish effective
theories in the landscape from those in the swampland? Within the swampland program this

One of the central ideas of the swampland program is the swampland distance conjecture,
which motivates why most of its applications focus on the asymptotics of the moduli space.

• Swampland Distance Conjecture [31]: Consider the moduli space of a consistent

• Conformal Field Theory Distance Conjecture [149]: All theories at infinite distance

Focusing on the second part of the swampland distance conjecture, a natural question that

• Emergent String Conjecture [153]: Any infinite distance limit in the moduli space of

lightest tower is that of particle excitations of a unique weakly coupled, asymptotically
tensionless Type II or heterotic string, accompanied by a tower of Kaluza-Klein states
with the same mass scale.

The interpretation of the states as Kaluza-Klein modes and particular types of strings assumes
a suitable choice of duality frame in which these modes admit a weakly coupled interpretation.
Note that these statements refer to the lightest towers of states and not the entire light spectrum.
For example, one may consider a decompactification at weak string coupling where the lightest
towers would be Kaluza-Klein modes, with fundamental string modes being light, but heavier
than them.

Most evidence for this conjecture has been collected within string theory and M-theory com-

can potentially be combined to gain a global understanding of the moduli space of string

swampland conjectures fall into these two categories. In fact, we will present two additional

global symmetries conjecture.

2.1.3 The No Global Symmetries Conjecture

Let us finish our review of swampland conjectures with one that is arguably one of the pillars
of the swampland program, although it actually predates it. For earlier related references, see,
for example, [180–182].

• No Global Symmetries Conjecture (e.g. [183]): A theory coupled to gravity cannot
have any exact global symmetries.

The conjecture is typically supported both by black hole and holographic arguments. For a
review of both and related references we refer the interested reader to e.g. [184].

In order to achieve absence of global symmetries, one has two options: breaking the symmetry
by introducing an appropriate object, a symmetry-breaking defect ∆, or gauging it. Let us
briefly summarize what we mean by those two options. Assume we have a p-form global
symmetry and an associated (p+ 1)-form conserved current J satisfying

d ∗ J = 0 . (2.5)

Explicitly breaking the symmetry by a charged defect ∆ implies that the conservation law is
no longer satisfied

Applying the above conjecture implies that when encountering a global symmetry in an effective
field theory, one must either find an object responsible for its breaking or an appropriate gauge
field that may be coupled to it. It turns out that, although this is a simple line of reasoning,
its predictive power is limited, so a more fruitful approach has been to consider more general
notions of conserved charges, namely higher-form topological charges. In the context of the
swampland program, the topological charges of most interest are the ones corresponding to

This line of research has been very successful in predicting and classifying objects in string

which concerns curvature singularities located at finite spacetime distance and interprets the

Although this is by no means a complete list of conjectures, the reader has by now seen some of

recurring theme has been the prediction of the appearance of new particles, typically organized
in towers, or extended objects. So far, very little has been said about how these degrees of
freedom affect the validity of the effective theory.

2.2 Species Scale

We have anticipated that the swampland distance conjecture [31] signifies a breakdown of the
effective field theory, but we have not yet quantified this statement. In quantum gravity appli-
cations, the ultraviolet cutoff, understood as the energy scale at which quantum gravitational
effects can no longer be considered suppressed, is typically referred to as the species scale [196,
197]. We will now proceed to review and contrast the various definitions and interpretations
of the species scale, before providing an additional interpretation of it in the context of the
Emergence Proposal in section 3.1. In that context, it will no longer be understood as a Wilso-
nian cutoff, but as the energy scale distinguishing between perturbative and non-perturbative
degrees of freedom.

Taking into account the bounds imposed by the heating of neutron stars by surrounding clouds

imposing that a single extra dimension is opening up at the micrometer scale, the so-called
dark dimension.3 In this case, the theory’s species scale is the five-dimensional Planck scale.

An appealing aspect of this scenario is that the Kaluza-Klein modes of the graviton can be
natural dark matter candidates [225, 231]. Primordial black holes [232] or axions [233] could
also play such a role. In fact, five-dimensional primordial black holes and a gas of massive
Kaluza–Klein gravitons were found to be equivalent [234]. In addition, the recent results of
the DESI collaboration [235, 236] indicate that the dark energy might be varying dynamically,
something that can be seen as a prediction of this scenario where the size of the single large
extra dimension evolves along its potential [237]. For reviews on the implications of this
proposal see e.g. [99, 238].

We would like to close this review of the dark dimension scenario by highlighting a related
paradox. Although the swampland principles used in its formulation are natural from a string-
theoretic point of view, a string-theoretic setup realizing the dark dimension scenario has
so far not been constructed in a controlled manner. See, however, [239–243] for concrete
top-down attempts and [244] for considerations related to its potential embedding in grand
unified theories, namely theories unifying gauge interactions in a single gauge group. Even
without a controlled top-down construction available, phenomenological aspects, such as the
interplay of neutrino masses and the cosmological constant in such a setup can be studied
[245].

Given that the predicted deviations from Newton’s law are investigated by various groups
(e.g. [246]), it remains to be seen whether this scenario will survive experimental tests and
what this will teach us about dark matter and quantum gravity!

2.4 The Emergence Proposal

So far quantum gravity has warned us that effective field theories at infinite geodesic distances
in the moduli space cannot be trusted due to the appearance of infinitely many light states
organized in towers by some typical mass gap. The lightest of these towers have been identified
by the emergent string conjecture and the energy at which the initial effective description
breaks down has been quantified by the species scale. In the previous discussion, however, the
species scale was not treated as a Wilsonian cutoff in the usual sense, since states saturating
the cutoff were still included, while no general prescription for integrating out states appearing
in towers was specified. The absence of exact global symmetries may also be understood as a
prediction of the existence of objects or couplings ensuring their breaking or gauging. What
remains lacking is a unified dynamical principle explaining the appearance of these towers and
their relation to the low-energy couplings.

3Nevertheless, see also [229, 230] for considerations of two large extra dimensions.



The Emergence Proposal 65

A bold conjecture aspiring to tackle these fundamental questions is the Emergence Proposal.
Before providing in section 3.1 a view of the Emergence Proposal in M-theory, we will review
the historical development of the concept in the context of quantum gravity and string theory.
Its original formulation (later referred to as strong version [204]) is based on earlier results
e.g [247–249] and states the following.

• Emergence Proposal [33]: The dynamics (kinetic terms) for all fields are emergent in
the infrared by integrating out towers down from an ultraviolet scale Λ, which is below
the Planck scale.

This is a simple statement with very deep consequences, since it is not restricted to quantum
corrections to a pre-existing term, as renormalization in particle physics would typically suggest.
Instead, it postulates that there is no kinetic term in the ultraviolet to begin with. Possible
interpretations for this reasoning are that the overarching ultraviolet theory is of topological
nature or that it originates from a more exotic structure, potentially including no local degrees
of freedom. In fact, we have already encountered such a structure, matrix models, in section
1.5.1. Setting aside for the moment these fundamental issues, let us review how this conjecture
resonates with the swampland statements for d-dimensional effective field theories we have
already reviewed. In what follows we will be identifying Λ with the species scale.4 For the
moment, we will be truncating the towers at the species scale, as we have done for determining
the species scale itself.

Since the proposal was initially formulated for kinetic terms, whose form is encoded in the field
space metric, a natural question is if it can potentially be understood as a statement equivalent

from providing the dynamical interpretation of various statements we have encountered in

reconstructing various terms in the low-energy action by identifying the light spectrum of the
theory and integrating it out appropriately. Finally, the proposal seems to also resonate with
certain black hole results [210, 258, 259].

Let us summarize some of the central issues we have identified at the moment. The Emergence
Proposal is a deep statement about the effects of light states present in quantum gravity theories.
In the original formulation we have presented so far, it seems to face obstacles to being precisely
applied in both emergent string and decompactification limits, the only two possibilities allowed
by the emergent string conjecture. One could naively conclude that the only problem is that
this quantum field theory-inspired statement is simply not compatible with string modes. We
will argue that this conclusion is premature. Imposing a hard cutoff and restricting calculations
to states below that has been contested generally both in the context of gauge theories e.g. in
[260] (or more recently in [261] and in references therein) and in the context of quantum
gravitational applications e.g. [32, 262, 263].7 Additionally, it seems unlikely that modular
invariance can be reconciled with a truncation of towers, given the definitions of most modular
forms we have encountered so far in terms of infinite summations over the full Hilbert space
or at least full subsectors thereof.

7Moreover, also in the context of the Emergence Proposal itself, in footnote46 of [33], where the formulation
