implied. The applications in [248] are also compatible with this direction.



The Emergence Proposal 69

The next logical step would be to attempt to modify the original proposal. One avenue is
to try to weaken the original statement. Attempting to recover the modular dependence of
leading-order corrections to pre-existing tree-level terms in such a way (called weak emergence
in [204]) has been a very fruitful avenue on which most early applications of the proposal were
focused [33, 118, 151, 204, 253–257]. For more recent developments see also [167, 264–268].

However, since some of the obstructions already outlined affect also this more modest proposal
(see e.g. the gauge coupling considerations in [165]), we would like to focus on the original
(strong) formulation.

The remainder of the thesis is organized as follows:

• In section 3.1, we will introduce an M-theoretic refinement of the original Emergence
Proposal, also following the review [269]. We will shift our focus from subtleties of
other approaches to analogies with the development of string theory, drawing upon
the results of [270]. Concretely, after detecting the most appropriate M-theory limit
for the Emergence Proposal, we will identify as perturbative the states whose typical
mass scale is not above the species scale in that limit. Since the limit will correspond
to a decompactification of the M-theory circle with other compact volumes being fixed,
these particle states will be Kaluza-Klein modes and particles obtained from branes not
wrapping the M-theory circle. As we will see, a realization of our refinement also requires
the introduction of an appropriate regularization technique. We will review in detail
our chosen method, which has the advantage that it allows one to keep track of the
physical origin of the various contributions to amplitudes. It is based on Schwinger-like
integral representations and includes minimal subtraction and analytic continuation
of infinite sums. This scheme will be essential for providing concrete evidence for our
claims. We will shortly review its first application to a non-compact example in section
3.2, for which the prescription was originally developed, the resolved conifold. Besides
supporting our claims concerning the Emergence Proposal, this application fills a related
gap in the literature by extending the integrating-out interpretation of non-perturbative
contributions to the prepotential to the perturbative terms, at least for the resolved
conifold.

• Focusing on toroidal compactifications, we will turn our attention to a gravitational and a
gauge coupling, whose structure is intricately related to certain automorphic forms. The
structure of those forms is to a large extent understood from the point of view of U-duality,
which we will shortly review in section 4.1. We will then show that our logic suggests an
extension of the spectrum integrated out in computations for the R4-term in section 4.2
based on [271]. This extension will allow us to reproduce the full coupling in dimensions
d = 7, 8 and by decompactification in 9, 10, while admitting an interpretation in terms of
the properties of the related automorphic form, which is a constrained Eisenstein series,
in dimensions d ≥ 4. Turning the logic around, in section 4.3, we will apply the same
methods to a gauge coupling, the F 4-term in six dimensions, where we will exhibit the
redundancy of certain degrees of freedom, following [272]. The combination of the two
applications is compelling evidence that our proposed refinement identifies precisely the
relevant perturbative spectrum, without under- or overestimating it. They also serve as
extensive checks of our refinement and regularization procedure, which proved to be
compatible with the properties of these automorphic forms.





Part II

The Emergence Proposal in M-Theory





Chapter 3

An M-theoretic Refinement of Emergence

We will begin the main part of the present thesis by motivating an M-theoretic refinement of
the Emergence Proposal. Rather than focusing on the various obstacles already encountered,
we will follow a constructive approach, arguing that its central idea is compatible with funda-
mental aspects of string and M-theory, as well as aspects of particle physics, such as quantum
electrodynamics. We will then motivate the regularization technique used in our applications,
illustrating this prescription in the non-compact resolved conifold example in section 3.2.3.

3.1 Overview and Formulation of Refinement

The Emergence Proposal is a very attractive statement for a quantum gravity theory, as its
starting point is the expectation that geometry is a quantum effect. This seems unlikely to be
compatible with a typical perturbation theory, where one works with quantum corrections to a
pre-existing classical background. It is therefore expected that both a usual effective theory
prescription and perturbative string theory will be challenged by it.

We have already encountered a theory which, despite appearing in the framework of string
theory, is not captured by its perturbative expansion and in fact seems to require a completely
different treatment to be perturbatively quantized, M-theory. In what follows, we will propose
a refinement of the Emergence Proposal in M-theory. In doing so, we will provide a concrete
suggestion for which states are to be integrated out for the computation of observables, drawing
on lessons from string theory. Ultimately, such a proposal should be formulated in terms of the
fundamental degrees of freedom of M-theory and, ideally, should not rely on supersymmetry.
As a quantized perturbative theory of M-theory has not been formulated (yet), we will content
ourselves with statements at the level of type IIA objects and the corresponding particles
obtained from them. Note that to ease notation from now on we will denote MPl,11 =M∗.

• Emergence Proposal (M-theory) [269]: In the infinite distance limit to M-theory
M∗R11 ≫ 1, approached by keeping the d-dimensional Planck scale constant and com-
pactification cycles at order O(1) in eleven-dimensional Planck units M∗, a perturbative
quantum gravity theory arises whose low-energy effective description emerges via quan-
tum effects by integrating out the full infinite towers of states with a typical mass scale
parametrically not larger than the 11D Planck scale. These are Kaluza-Klein modes and
transversally wrapped M2- and M5-branes carrying momentum along the eleventh
direction.

with mass scale above the species scale cannot be included in perturbative calculations. This is
similar to how in type II string theories on a compact background, although all string winding
modes would be considered, Dp-branes would not be included in a perturbative amplitude.

This brief analysis demonstrates how the same Schwinger proper-time representation (upon
appropriate regularization) contains both the perturbative weak-field expansion, arising from
a power expansion in E, and the non-perturbative contributions associated with the pole
structure of the integrand. Recall that imaginary contributions to the action are signals of
instability of the chosen background and in this case Schwinger interpreted this instability as
an electron-positron pair appearing from the vacuum, a highly non-trivial result at the time.

The previous discussion focuses on the simplest case of vanishing magnetic field and spinor
quantum electrodynamics, but a more general pedagogical overview may be found in [287],
which also discusses different regularization methods for the resulting expressions. This
calculation is an example of the background-field method: the electron is quantized while the
electromagnetic field is treated as a prescribed classical background.

In the following sections, we will apply an analogous strategy in different settings. We will be
taking advantage of similar representations of our amplitudes to identify both perturbative and
non-perturbative contributions while applying an appropriate regularization technique.

NS5-branes and Kaluza-Klein states as well. Additionally, a formula to extract directly the
degeneracy of states (whose weighted sum enters the Gopakumar-Vafa invariants) on K3-fibered
Calabi-Yau threefolds has been conjectured in [311] (building on [312]) and tested recently in
[313]. The growth of Gopakumar-Vafa invariants has also been used to collect evidence in favor
of the emergent string conjecture [162]. Finally, we note that the Gopakumar-Vafa formula has
been studied and extended in the context of the near-horizon geometry of BPS black holes in
[314–316], using semiclassical complex saddles.

3.2.3 M-theoretic Emergence Proposal on the Resolved Conifold

The conifold plays an important role in the local description of compact Calabi-Yau manifolds
close to singularities. Zooming into the vicinity of the singularity leads to considering non-
compact Calabi-Yau spaces. Although gravity decouples in the strict non-compact limit of the
manifold8, they still exhibit interesting properties, for example through wrapped Dp-branes at
singularities.

Considering the standard complex coordinates {X,Y, U, V } on C4, the conifold is a singular
non-compact Calabi-Yau, which has a singularity at the origin. Locally, the vicinity of the
singularity is described by

XY − UV = 0 . (3.47)

A neighborhood of the conifold locus may be thought of as a cone over S2 × S3. One can
either deform (3.47) or resolve the singularity by replacing it locally with an S2 ∼= P1 (for more
details see e.g. [288] or Appendix A.3 for an analogous discussion of the K3 surface). These
two options give rise to the deformed and the resolved conifold. The latter is the geometry of
interest here.

Although the resolved conifold has been a conveniently simple setup to test our claims both for
the spectrum of light states required to obtain complete results via an integrating-out procedure
and for the suggested regularization scheme, one would naturally like to explore more realistic
compactifications. To generalize the analysis to a compact Calabi-Yau threefold Y , one considers
the limit ti → λti with λ → ∞ and i = 1, . . . , h1,1(Y ). With the four-dimensional dilaton
kept constant, this limit is equivalent to the decompactification limit to five dimensions of
M-theory on Y × S1.

The light particle degrees of freedom would now include D2-D0 bound states wrapping all
2-cycles in the homology latticeH2(Y,Z). Then, one must sum over them in the Schwinger-like
integral so that the result will be sensitive to all Kähler moduli ti. This means that the full
topological amplitude F1, including the linear terms, will emerge from a Schwinger one-loop
computation. Notice that the concrete evaluation might require yet another regularization
for the sum over the linear terms in the Kähler moduli. As previously speculated, we may
consider also contributions from BPS states involving NS5-branes and Kaluza-Klein modes
along Y . Determining their finite contributions requires a proper quantization of the wrapped
NS5-branes, which has so far been out of reach. Moreover, the general Schwinger integral
(3.40) contains contributions from the r = 1 sector, associated with genus 1 curves in Y . Such
states contribute to Fg for g ≥ 1.

Significant progress has been achieved in extending this computation to the quintic and several
further Calabi-Yau examples. This included a regularization of the sums over Gopakumar-Vafa
invariants required for computing triple intersection numbers appearing in F0 as emergent via
an integrating-out procedure in the suggested M-theory limit [322]. This result was further
elaborated on in [323], where the same methodology was also applied to F1. Naturally, one
would like to consider increasingly more complicated setups and different couplings, however
this is of significant computational difficulty. For instance, an Emergence Proposal-inspired
integrating-out procedure has to this day not yet been applied in the context of Calabi-Yau
fourfolds although their enumerative geometry contains invariants of similar structure [324].
We further note that in [264–266], analytic continuation of the integrals to complex proper
time was suggested for the study of non-perturbative results, in a sense in the same spirit as
our discussion of electron pair production.

Before considering further applications of the M-theoretic Emergence Proposal, let us address
a final issue in the context of type IIA Calabi-Yau compactifications. Namely, let us verify why
the observed success of our integrating-out procedure is indeed special to M-theory and cannot
straightforwardly be extended to e.g. emergent string limits, as our refinement suggests.

M-theoretic Emergence and Eisenstein Series

In this chapter, we will consider applications of the M-theoretic Emergence Proposal in compact-
ifications with maximal and half-maximal supersymmetry. Although section 4.2 will concern a
gravitational coupling, theR4-term, and section 4.3 will concern a gauge coupling, the F 4-term,
the mathematical structure of the two amplitudes is in fact quite similar and related to the
structure of U-duality groups. For this reason, we will begin with some mathematical prelimi-
naries, before proceeding to the main results, which will rely on their integral representations
in terms of Schwinger-like integrals, to which our previously outlined methodology will be
applied. We assume the reader is familiar with aspects of representation theory.

From a physical perspective, for the R4-term our refinement will suggest an extension of the
integrated-out spectrum of light particle states appearing in its computations, while for the
F 4-term a reduction thereof. Given these two complementary results, this chapter provides
substantial evidence that our prescription correctly identifies the perturbative particle states in
the M-theory limit of interest. It also illustrates the power of our regularization scheme, which
allows working with expansions making the properties of the corresponding automorphic
forms evident.

4.1 U-duality and Eisenstein Series

Let us consider M-theory compactified on a torus Tn. We have already discussed that such
a compactification would preserve maximal supersymmetry and encountered a symmetry of
this theory when viewed as the strongly coupled limit of type IIA on Tn−1, which is T-duality.
It turns out that the quantum symmetry of such a setup is actually U-duality [330], some
properties of which we will review here, mainly following [191, 331].

In order to identify the quantum symmetries of a theory, one needs to consider not only the
low-energy effective action, but also the spectrum. More concretely, by compactifying type
IIA string theory on Tn−1, one might naively expect that this theory is symmetric under
O(n− 1, n− 1,R) by considering momentum and winding modes classically. If one, however,
takes into account that momentum and winding are quantized and that the determinant-(−1)
elements of O(n, n,Z) flip chirality, therefore exchanging the theory to type IIB as we have
seen, one would consider SO(n− 1, n− 1,Z) as the appropriate T-duality group. However,
this would not necessarily be the correct quantum symmetry if it did not preserve the lattice of
Dp-brane charges, which it does.

A property that will be particularly relevant for us is that the U-duality groups exhibit a nested
structure, namely that they are related by a process of group disintegration reflecting the

highest weights as linear combinations with positive integer coefficients of the fundamental
weights dual to the simple roots.

Let us focus on the three Dynkin nodes, the deletion of which gives rise to subgroups (more
precisely maximal parabolic subgroups) of interest for physical applications. Their dual weights
can be related to BPS objects and their descendants lying in the same orbit.

• The fundamental weight λ(0) corresponds to the tension of anM2-brane and is associated
with the membrane multiplet.

• The fundamental weight, typically denoted as λ(1) corresponds to the tension of an
M2-brane wrapped on one direction and is associated with the so-called string multiplet.

• The fundamental weight λ(n−1) corresponds to the mass scale of a Kaluza-Klein mode
and is associated with the particle multiplet.

like [333] one often considers M-theory as compactified on Tn+1, distinguishing the M-theory
circle.

Recall how the geometrization of the SL(2,Z) symmetry of type IIB gives rise to F-theory.
Geometrizing the T-duality group SO(n, n,Z) gives rise to double field theory [334] (see [273]
for a review). As the name suggests, this can be thought of as a doubling of the coordinates,
since the winding modes are geometrized, namely new coordinates dual to them are introduced.
Extending this to also geometrize any other quantum charge in the U-duality group gives
rise to exceptional field theory [335]. To restrict field dependencies on a physical subspace of
the enlarged space we described, one imposes the so-called section conditions. These can be
understood as a projection onto some representation of the duality group and in the examples
we will consider they are equivalent to the 1/2-BPS conditions.

4.2 R4-Terms in M-Theory

We will now review how the structure of a higher-curvature correction in toroidal compact-
ifications of M-theory, namely, the R4-term, serves as a manifestation of the M-theoretic
Emergence Proposal, applying the regularization prescriptions that we developed and have
already reviewed in the context of the resolved conifold. This section is based on [271]. Given
the peculiarity of the limit of interest, namely the fact that we will be working in a regime
where the volumes are O(1) in M-theory units, an important factor for considering such a
quantity is that it is believed to enjoy protection by supersymmetry [344]. It is precisely thanks
to this property that we can trust these results even in our M-theory limit, without knowing
the quantized spectrum that would allow perturbative computations there.

As reviewed in Appendix D, solving a linear Diophantine equation in k variables requires the
introduction of k − 1 integers for the Kaluza-Klein momenta mI . This corresponds to the
situation in which all k winding numbers are non-vanishing. Setting any winding number
to zero leads to the corresponding Kaluza-Klein momentum being unconstrained, so that we

of vanishing nI as described by a vector α, the only exception being the case in which all of
them are vanishing as there is no Diophantine equation to be solved anymore. Physically,
this corresponds to the pure Kaluza-Klein sector of the computation. We will not consider
this sector in what follows, but rather assume that at least one of the winding numbers is
non-vanishing. We will now show that the constant contribution, 2π2/3, is related to extended
objects, in this case strings, a point that will also be crucial for our M-theoretic implications.

predicted by the M-theoretic refinement of the Emergence Proposal, however, a precise check
has not been performed to this day. Importantly, due to the different BPS orbit, the extension
of our results to this term would be non-trivial. If successful, such an extension should provide
all terms, namely, in this case, tree-level, two-loop and non-perturbative contributions.

For higher-derivative couplings the situation becomes more complicated. One way to see
this is the fact that the corresponding amplitude does not satisfy a Laplace equation, but a
Poisson one, at least in some examples studied in the literature like ∇6R4 [336, 357], which
is 1/8-BPS. Given the fact that the Poisson equation and the various parabolic expansions of
the amplitude contain combinations of Eisenstein series we have already encountered, it is
tempting to speculate that our M-theoretic refinement will also be testable in those examples at
the level of the various terms, however, an explicit test has not been performed yet. In fact, these
expressions are not straightforwardly encoded in a single integral representation or a simple
product thereof, but this might be achievable using the spectral methods of [358].8 Interestingly,
in [359], a general study of the automorphic forms appearing in higher curvature corrections in
toroidal compactifications of M-theory suggested the appearance of a distinguished fundamental

significantly more involved, as potentially infinite loops would need to be considered.

Rather than attempting to verify these conjectures by extending the analysis to further gravita-

mathematical structure.

Conclusions and Outlook

Let us conclude by summarizing our findings and what we have learned about the role of
emergence in the swampland program and M-theory.

In the present thesis, we focused on a particular realization of the concept of emergence,
as originally inspired by the Emergence Proposal, formulated within the framework of the
swampland program. The original proposal postulated that kinetic terms could be derived as
quantum effects via an integrating-out procedure, however it was later interpreted as not being
solely restricted to kinetic terms.

Our goal was to refine this notion into a version that could recover complete results, rather
than leading-order estimates of corrections to pre-existing terms. This was realized in perhaps
one of the most surprising corners of the string theory framework, M-theory. We identified
an isotropic decompactification limit to this eleven-dimensional theory as the most relevant
for extracting maximum information from amplitudes in an integrating-out manner, while
providing a concrete regularization algorithm to perform these calculations. In that case,
although the eleventh direction was decompactifying, all other compact directions were kept
fixed in M-theory units. This implied that only Kaluza-Klein modes and branes not wrapping
the large eleventh direction would become light when approaching the decompactification
limit.

Our motivation for how to work with the spectrum identified as light and therefore perturbative
relied heavily on string-theoretic amplitudes, rather than the Wilsonian approach to effective
field theories. This implied that the quantum gravity cutoff, the species scale, which in this case
was the eleven-dimensional Planck scale, was understood as characterizing towers appearing at
the asymptotics of the moduli space as perturbative or not and not as a hard cutoff. Concretely,
entire particle towers were being integrated out, rather than being truncated at some energy
level.

On a conceptual level, we explored how our refinement appears, in our opinion, as compatible
with the physical structure of M-theory and how it may also be used as inspiration to extract
more information regarding its potential perturbative quantization, which still lies beyond
current techniques. In doing so, we commented on how our ideas regarding the fact that
M2- and M5- branes should be considered on equal footing conceptually interplay with
membrane physics, conformal field theories, matrix models etc. On a technical level, we
followed a pragmatic approach of calculating supersymmetrically protected amplitudes using
only the light particle spectrum obtained by wrapping the corresponding light branes on
compact directions. As a first application, we verified that our refinement and regularization
prescription can give rise to the full results for the prepotential of the resolved conifold. These
importantly included also the (unambiguous) perturbative terms. The last part of the thesis
was focusing on toroidal compactifications, examining a gravitational and a gauge coupling



156 Conclusions and Outlook

whose mathematical structure was found to be compatible with our M-theoretic Emergence
Proposal in a highly non-trivial manner.

Our prescription suggested an extension of the integrated-out spectrum for the R4-coupling in
toroidal compactifications of M-theory compared to previous attempts to describe it via super-
gravity calculations focusing only on Kaluza-Klein modes. It was verified that the extension
to light particles obtained from M2- and M5-branes wrapping compact cycles but not the
M-theory circle produces the complete results expected from string-theoretic amplitudes down
to 7D, while we argued that we expect the result to hold up to 4D. To achieve this, we examined
the expected instanton spectrum and analyzed how our findings are compatible with more
formal conjectures relating the amplitude to constrained Eisenstein series of maximal parabolic
subgroups of U-duality groups in dimensions down to 4D. Contributions not reproduced directly
were related to the presence of extended objects and obtained systematically in the decompact-
ification limits of lower-dimensional results. For an F 4-gauge coupling in 6D heterotic/type
IIA theories, our refinement of the Emergence Proposal proposed a reduction of the spectrum
of states contributing to the amplitude, which we verified through the cancellations of heavy,
from our point of view non-perturbative, contributions of M5-branes also wrapping the large
eleventh direction. Similar to the computations for the R4-term, although we were considering
the light spectrum in our decompactification limit, the results were exact. In both cases, the
analysis was performed in rectangular tori, but we expect the results to remain valid upon
including non-trivial Kalb-Ramond fields.

The applications presented in this thesis provide strong indications that we have managed to
identify the precise fundamental particle spectrum for these protected couplings in M-theory
compactifications in our proposed limit, not a sub- or superset. Hence, we have encountered
an instance where the swampland program has motivated a new look at established aspects of
string-theoretic calculations. Our developed regularization scheme, which included minimal
subtraction and analytic continuation, was crucial in keeping track of the physical origin
of the various contributions appearing in Schwinger-like integrals describing the examined
amplitudes. Such a scheme would not have been available if we had insisted on treating the
species scale as a strict cutoff.

Nevertheless, we view these results as the beginning rather than the end of the story. On a
realistic level, our checks had to begin from well-controlled setups, which is why we focused on
supersymmetrically protected terms that were not receiving perturbative corrections beyond
one loop. This restriction to protected observables is natural, since our limit does not lie in
a parametrically controlled eleven-dimensional supergravity regime, making quantities with
strong non-renormalization properties particularly valuable probes. Although even then the
resulting expressions were convoluted, highlighting the non-triviality of our regularization
prescription, in the future one would need to consider further extensions to more generic
terms. Additionally, recalling that the initial motivation for the Emergence Proposal was also
to provide a tool to derive other swampland constraints, it would be interesting to revisit how
this can happen at least in our limit of interest, for example for some versions of the weak
gravity conjecture.

Let us provide some examples of the impact of the presented results. In the context of phe-
nomenology, recently, we presented a very bold application of the Emergence Proposal, in
which the limit of interest to us throughout this thesis was related to the Dark Dimension



Conclusions and Outlook 157

Scenario [360], thus relating our considerations to phenomenology. Although this application
is highly speculative, it also highlights that, at least at the moment, our refinement stands
as one of the few remaining candidates for performing perturbative calculations, or at least
estimates thereof, in an intrinsically M-theoretic regime. The ultimate goal would be, of course,
to reformulate the conjecture purely in terms of M-theoretic degrees of freedom, letting go of
the type IIA intuition, and use it as a building tool for the corresponding theory. Due to the
lack of a microscopic description of M-theory, this remains a formidable task. In that context,
on a conceptual level, the works presented in this thesis motivated revisiting the BFSS matrix
model and exploring potential M5-brane extensions thereof without changing the theory’s
background [277].

We therefore propose to view the present thesis as a detailed invitation to reconsider what
information about M-theory is within our reach. From its potential applications in the swamp-
land program or phenomenology to formal aspects of membrane quantization, it clearly has
many lessons waiting to emerge!

Appendix D

Linear Diophantine Equations

Diophantine equations are polynomial equations with integer coefficients and for which one
is interested in integer solutions. They owe their name to the mathematician Diophantus of
Alexandria, who first studied them in the 3rd century. Despite the fact that they have been
continuously studied since then, it was only in the 20th century that it was proved that there
is no general algorithm determining whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation admits an
integer solution. This is the content of the MRDP theorem, named after the authors’ initials
[369], motivated by Hilbert’s tenth problem in mathematics. Fortunately, the situation is under
control for linear Diophantine equations. Since quadratic BPS conditions (e.g. (4.4)) appearing
in our analysis can be treated as such in our computations, in this appendix we present a brief
overview of linear Diophantine equations and how to solve them. More information can be
found, for example, in the classic reference [370].

The simplest instance is a linear Diophantine equation in two variables,X and Y , of the form

aX + bY = c, a, b, c ∈ Z, a or b ̸= 0. (D.1)

It is a theorem (e.g. Theorem 1, chapter 5 of [370]) that this equation admits integer solutions
iff gcd(a, b) divides c. If c = 0, the general solution is X = Nb, Y = −Na with N ∈ Z. If
c ̸= 0, the general solution is

X = X0 +Nb , Y = Y0 −Na , (D.2)

where (X0, Y0) is any solution of (D.1). Notice that one can assume gcd(a, b) = 1 from the
start without loss of generality. Indeed, if this condition is not met, one can divide (D.1) by
g2 ≡ gcd(a, b) > 1 to get ãX + b̃Y = c̃, with ã = a/g2 and similarly for b̃, c̃ and recover
again a linear Diophantine equation with coprime coefficients. The solution in the case g2 > 1
is given by replacing a → a/g2 and b → b/g2 in (D.2). Since this observation is valid for
any number of variables, we will systematically start with coprime coefficients. Knowing the
solution to the linear Diophantine equation in two variables, one can iterate the algorithm and
solve linear Diophantine equations in more variables.

The next step is to consider the homogeneous linear Diophantine equation in three variables

aX + bY + cZ = 0 , a, b, c ∈ Z, a or b or c ̸= 0 . (D.3)

abstracts.value: Rydberg atomic quantum receivers (RAQR) exhibit exceptional sensitivity to radio-frequency (RF) signals, positioning them as promising candidates for next-generation wireless systems. Extending their capabilities to orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM), however, requires atomic responses that go beyond broadband reception and are tailored to the structured interference of multicarrier signals. To bridge this gap, we develop an atomic-comb Rydberg receiver based on six-wave mixing (SWM) transduction. In particular, injecting a multi-tone local oscillator (LO) into the RAQR generates frequency-shifted replicas of the intrinsic SWM response. By subtly tuning the amplitude and phase of each LO tone, constructive and destructive interference can be selectively induced to preserve desired response components while attenuating harmful frequency offsets. Furthermore, we harness the response-reshaping capability of the proposed atomic comb to proactively mitigate OFDM interference. More explicitly, by exploiting the discrete difference-frequency structure of both carrier-frequency-offset (CFO)-induced and phase-noise (PN)-induced inter-carrier interference (ICI), we optimize the atomic-comb response to suppress dominant ICI components directly. We further reveal an intrinsic coupling between spectral shaping and the time-domain effective channel memory, motivating a joint optimization of both ICI and inter-symbol interference (ISI), which simultaneously suppresses inter-carrier leakage and post-cyclic-prefix (CP) tail energy. Extensive simulation results validate our atomic-comb design, unveiling that the proposed atomic comb can effectively reshape the receiver response over the OFDM, while mitigating ICI, shortening the effective channel memory, and substantially lowering CP overhead.

titles.title: Rydberg Atomic Quantum Receivers for OFDM Systems: An Atomic-Comb Design

abstracts.value: Can quantum communication determine the size of an anonymous network when no size bound is known? Classical impossibility proofs rely on the covering lemma: an execution can be reproduced on a larger network with the same local structure. Quantum interference invalidates this argument - a measurement record possible on a network can become impossible on a cover. We show that the impossibility of exact counting nevertheless survives. Our main result is a quantum analogue of the covering lemma that preserves local possibilities rather than complete executions. Within a cyclic covering family, every local measurement outcome possible at a node remains possible at a corresponding node in every sufficiently large network. This holds even after information has travelled around the smaller network, beyond the reach of a simple locality argument. We extend the principle to the universal covering tree and finite covers with sufficiently long cycles. The proof combines tensor-network methods with graph coverings: a common representation across network sizes turns normalization into a constraint on which local outcomes can occur. For uniform synchronous protocols with independently prepared nodes, this support-lifting principle rules out zero-error counting and even the production of a guaranteed finite size bound on anonymous rings and the other cyclic covering families considered here. It also rules out exact leader election with termination in finite time with probability one on these families. Measurements, classical control, and local memory growing with time are allowed; no predetermined running-time bound is assumed. Quantum interference thus defeats execution lifting without enabling infallible certification of network size.

titles.title: A Quantum Analogue of the Covering Lemma: Limits of Exact Anonymous Computation

abstracts.value: Ordinal optimization selects designs that are good enough rather than optimal when evaluation is expensive and the budget is small. The alignment probability measures the chance that the selected set contains at least a prescribed number of truly good designs. We formulate quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems that maximize this probability under a fixed oracle budget. We study exact, coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design as a first instance, with the budget counted in comparison queries. For every classical comparison budget smaller than the number of designs, we prove that a knockout among uniformly sampled designs attains the optimum. The sample is drawn without replacement and contains one more design than the number of comparisons. For a uniformly random order, the selected design's rank has a polynomial probability law. At the same comparison budget, the maximum quantum degree is at most twice the classical maximum, a factor attained whenever there are more than twice as many designs as comparisons, so a quantum algorithm can realize rank laws that no classical algorithm with the same budget can. We determine the exact quantum optimum with one comparison for every number of designs and every good-enough set. For selecting the best of n designs, the optimal success probability with one quantum comparison is approximately 3.30/n for large n, compared with 2/n for one classical comparison. When the best design is sought, one quantum comparison gives a higher alignment probability than two classical comparisons whenever there are more than nine designs.

titles.title: Quantum ordinal optimization under a fixed comparison budget

abstracts.value: Supervised machine learning in high-energy physics (HEP) requires training on labeled simulations of particle collisions, which are known to be unfaithful to the underlying physics. This leads to significant inaccuracies and biases in the transfer of trained models to real data, limiting the power of deep learning methods. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a promising alternative for pretraining directly on real, unlabeled data. However, existing techniques largely operate with inductive biases inspired by domains such as images and natural language. We propose RINO (Renormalization Group DIstillation with NO Labels), which, for the first time, exploits the fundamentally multi-scale renormalization group structure of high-energy jet formation as a physically grounded source of SSL views. We define teacher-student representations across energy scales using different levels of hierarchical clustering, aligned via DINO-style self-distillation. To mirror the background-dominated nature of real collider data, RINO pretrains exclusively on jets from quantum chromodynamics (QCD) processes and is evaluated on out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer to rare signal classes. In our controlled data-efficiency study, RINO matches fully supervised training on JetNet after finetuning on only 1% of the labeled data. With the full labeled dataset, RINO improves OOD classification accuracy on top-quark jets by 5.9% and, without retraining, improves AUC on the unseen Higgs boson decay channel $H \to 4q$ by 4.1% over the strongest SSL baseline. Scale-structure diagnostics reveal that DINO-style self-distillation permits our backbone to retain scale-dependent structure. Ablation studies show that this accounts for an 8.6% OOD accuracy gap with respect to alternative SSL paradigms such as SimCLR. Code is available at https://github.com/zichunhao/RINO.

titles.title: RINO: Renormalization Group Distillation with No Labels

abstracts.value: A multiple-access channel transmits messages from several senders to one receiver. For quantum outputs, the receiver must distinguish states depending on all messages, while tests for different decoding errors may not commute. In this paper, we give a self-contained account of simultaneous decoding, in which one joint measurement recovers the messages at the established achievable rates using independent codebooks. The proof combines Sen's tilted-subspace method with Cheng's analysis of the pretty-good measurement, a standard measurement for distinguishing quantum states. Auxiliary labels close to a common reference state separate the geometric directions associated with different errors. A Gram-matrix bound then allows separately chosen binary tests to certify the performance of one measurement. The labels are removed from the completed decoder, leading to a deterministic packing theorem that applies to finite state ensembles, including unequal priors. We develop the two-sender case first, with worked examples and figures, before treating any fixed number of senders. Sharper finite-error guarantees for the same decoder are developed separately, with sharp bounds for two specified steps of the analysis rather than a claim of globally optimal decoding. Applications recover known achievable rates for unassisted and entanglement-assisted classical communication, distributed classical compression with quantum side information, and coherent-state communication through a beamsplitter or passive multiport device. The common proof makes the geometric mechanism and its quantitative consequences available without repeating the construction for each application.

titles.title: Quantum simultaneous decoding via pretty-good measurements of tilted states

abstracts.value: High-pileup conditions in CMS during the HL-LHC era make charged-particle tracking increasingly challenging as detector occupancy and combinatorics grow. We present a hybrid approach that exploits Line Segment Tracking (LST) objects rather than individual hits to enable the first CMS ML-based track reconstruction algorithm. The LST objects, namely the triplets used in this study, are built according to geometry- and physics-driven criteria and carry richer local structure, geometrical cues, and physics quantities such as transverse momentum, which helps the model incorporate detector-level information from the start. We apply a Transformer encoder with geometrically masked sparse self-attention to embed these objects in a learned latent space, and use object condensation to assemble full tracks in a single inference step. This object-based representation reduces complexity in dense environments and makes the model less sensitive to ambiguities introduced by high pileup. Evaluated on CMS Phase-2 simulation of $t\bar{t}$ events at $\langle μ\rangle = 200$, the approach achieves reconstruction efficiency comparable to the LST quintuplet baseline while reducing the fake rate by roughly a factor of three and suppressing duplicates almost entirely, demonstrating the promise of advanced ML architectures for next-generation particle tracking.

titles.title: Using Line Segment Tracking to enable ML-based Track Reconstruction in CMS

abstracts.value: This paper explores topological phase transitions in the momentum space of the $κ$-deformed $ϕ^4$ lattice model within the mean-field approximation. We show that the double-well structure of the momentum space gives rise to degenerate momentum states at high energies and that this change is marked by a phase transition. We investigate this transition using both numerical and analytical methods, with the analytical approach based primarily on singularity theory. Our numerical analysis shows that the energy at which the topological phase transition occurs is related to the noncommutative parameter by the simple power law $E \sim 1/α^{4}$. By mapping the constant-energy-level surface to the $A_{3}$ singularity, we obtain the same result analytically. We also present results unique to noncommutative systems, showing that the fraction of particles in degenerate momentum states has a nonzero commutative limit. As a nonperturbative effect, this result provides a testable prediction for the existence of noncommutative spacetime.

titles.title: New topological phase transitions in $κ$-deformed $ϕ^4$ lattice models

abstracts.value: Stationary scattering admits a dynamical formulation in which the scattering data are extracted from the evolution operator for an effective non-stationary and non-unitary quantum system. This provides a mathematical method of solving scattering problems. We consider the possibility of realizing such a quantum system and relating the scattering information to outcomes of quantum measurements performed on it. To this end, we examine stationary scattering problems in one dimension where the scattering data consist of reflection and transmission amplitudes and the corresponding effective quantum system is a non-unitary two-level system. The states of this system identify points in a Bloch sphere $S^2$ and their evolution yields trajectories in $S^2$. Quantum measurements turn out to be capable of providing information about the reflection amplitudes. We identify configurations displaying reflectionlessness with situations where one or both of the poles of $S^2$ undergo cyclic evolutions. Spectral singularities and coherent perfect absorption correspond to dynamical spin flips which map one of the poles of $S^2$ to the other.

titles.title: Non-Stationary Quantum Systems Associated with Stationary Scattering in One Dimension

abstracts.value: We consider singular Schrödinger operators with an attractive $δ'$ interaction of strength $β$ supported by a star graph and prove that the ground-state eigenvalue is uniquely maximized by stars of the maximum symmetry. Two different proofs are presented, one for an even number of edges using a comparison to the $δ$ interaction star, the other general based on Birman-Schwinger technique.

abstracts.value: We study the entanglement structure of gravitons in quasicrystalline inflation. Both parity-even and parity-odd interactions generate graviton pairs with nonzero total momentum. For opposite-helicity pairs with identical momenta, the parity-even contribution can be nonzero, whereas the parity-odd contribution vanishes. The transition from inflation to radiation domination produces additional conventional two-mode squeezing. We derive the resulting normal and anomalous covariances. The initially nonzero reciprocal blocks of the full field-momentum covariance remain nonzero under homogeneous evolution, although individual components can vanish. We show that this homogeneous, helicity-preserving evolution acts unitarily within each helicity sector and therefore preserves the entanglement between the complete right- and left-helicity sectors. Nevertheless, it can eliminate entanglement in the reduced state of a co-propagating pair. We illustrate this distinction using a solvable four-mode model.

titles.title: Primordial Graviton Entanglement in Quasicrystalline Inflation

abstracts.value: Low-energy electrons in graphene obey an emergent, rotationally invariant Dirac equation, while the honeycomb lattice enters only through higher-order, symmetry-breaking corrections, the leading one being trigonal warping. This provides a unique solid-state arena to address a cornerstone challenge in quantum gravity: how to detect ultraviolet symmetry-breaking granular corrections, suppressed by a fundamental scale, atop an emergent infrared relativistic continuum. We show that intense counter-rotating $ω$-$2ω$ fields and valley-resolved high-harmonic generation (HHG) provide such a probe. Within a family of models that interpolates continuously between the isotropic Dirac cone and nearest-neighbour graphene at fixed Fermi velocity, the valley contrast of the harmonic yield vanishes identically in the symmetric theory, grows linearly with the warping coupling, and its valley-even counterpart appears only at second order, as expected from effective-field-theory power counting. The stronger the laser, the farther it drives electrons from the Dirac points, so the laser intensity plays the role of the collision energy. For the fourth harmonic, the leading warping correction alone accounts for the valley contrast of real graphene up to fundamental intensities of about $10^{11}$ W/cm$^2$, below the damage threshold of monolayer graphene, whereas the fifth harmonic already reveals higher-order lattice corrections at intensities around $10^{10}$ W/cm$^2$. The two harmonics, which rotate in opposite directions, are emitted by opposite valleys. Valley-resolved harmonics are far more sensitive than the residual valley populations, making them a practical detector of lattice-scale physics hidden beneath an emergent Dirac theory.

titles.title: Valley-resolved high harmonics probe symmetry breaking beyond the Dirac cone

abstracts.value: Quantum thermalization of closed systems -- i.e. the relaxation of local properties to their thermodynamic value along the Hamiltonian evolution -- is generically expected in non-integrable systems at finite energy density. In this work we show that quantum spin systems with at least one spin component coupled through long-range ferromagnetic interactions, and a second spin component coupled to a field, cannot in general thermalize to a paramagnetic state whenever they have a finite, negative energy per spin. The long-range interactions we consider decay as a power law of the distance, $\sim r^{-α}$ with $α< d$, where $d$ is the number of spatial dimensions of the system. The lack of thermalization is generic to an infinite family of Hamiltonians, and it is not associated to any form of integrability. It can instead be understood by the anomalous features of the thermodynamics of the system in the paramagnetic phase, which cannot be reflected in the properties of the eigenstates. This leads to a breakdown of eigenstate typicality and of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. Interestingly, the non-thermal states emerging at long times in the dynamics display long-range multipartite entanglement, elevating the breakdown of thermalization to a resource.

titles.title: Breakdown of thermalization in quantum spin systems with long-range interactions

abstracts.value: The structures in the di-J/psi spectrum seen at the LHC are widely read as fully charmed tetraquarks. As an alternative scenario, the $2^{++}$ production amplitude for a compact $cc\bar c\bar c$ source rescattering through ten charmonium-pair channels is presented. The model is completely fixed except for three background parameters and provides a competitive description of the data, with chi-sq/ndf=56/50. Prominent features are driven by J/psi psi(nS) thresholds or threshold enhancement, with no need for exotic hadrons.

abstracts.value: We review a many-body formulation of gravitational anomalies as obstructions to realizing the complete low-energy data by a local {\it bosonic} lattice quantum system of the same dimension. In this formulation, an anomalous theory can be realized at the boundary of a gapped {\it bosonic} lattice bulk, whose topological order gives a one-to-one classification of the anomaly. An invertible bulk reproduces conventional anomaly inflow; a bulk with non-trivial topological excitations yields a non-invertible generalization. To describe the holographic theory of anomalies, we explain the distinction between uniquely defined topological order and many versions of topological quantum field theory and discuss the boundary-to-bulk map. As an application of the holographic theory of anomalies, we describe morphisms between local quantum theories (such as quantum field theories). These morphisms are built from a bulk domain wall and an invertible boundary junction, which give rise to a sandwich picture. Chiral boson/fermion theory, Laughlin edges, and boundaries of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ higher gauge theory with bosonic or fermionic point-like excitations illustrate the different kinds of information about non-invertible anomalies contained in transport coefficients, superselection sectors, and condensation data. In particular, a fermionic theory can be viewed as a theory with a particular non-invertible gravitational anomaly. Those examples also reveal that {\it symmetry $\sim$ gravitational anomaly $\sim$ topological order in one higher dimension}.

titles.title: Holographic theory of non-invertible gravitational anomalies

abstracts.value: Three hadronic-bond mechanisms were proposed in our previous studies to describe near-threshold exotic hadrons in terms of hadronic molecular configurations: the covalent bond arises from the sharing and exchange of valence light quarks between hadronic clusters, the creation bond originates from the activation of coherent sea $q\bar{q}$ degrees of freedom followed by the formation of effective covalent correlations, and the annihilation bond arises from valence $q\bar{q}$ annihilation and the associated mixing with a nearby compact state. A simple toy model was previously constructed only for the covalent bond, and in the present study we extend this model to incorporate the creation and annihilation bonds within a unified framework. The resulting framework organizes covalent-bond configurations as tending to lie below threshold and creation-bond configurations as tending to appear above threshold, while the annihilation bond can shift a pre-existing molecular configuration either downward or upward through mixing with a nearby compact state. An effective activation energy $E_{\rm{act}}$ is introduced for the coherent sea four-quark component involved in the creation bond, with the $Z_c(3900)$ providing the benchmark value $E_{\rm{act}}\sim17~{\rm{MeV}}$. Intriguingly, this value is numerically close to the reported mass of the $X_{17}$ particle, which we previously interpreted as a low-energy bare four-quark structure. This numerical proximity may therefore reflect common low-energy (four-quark) dynamics, although the microscopic connection remains to be established. For the isoscalar $D^*\bar{D}^*B^*\bar{B}^*$ configuration involving the $Z_c(4020)$ and $Z_b(10650)$ creation-bond subsystems linked by two additional covalent bonds, we estimate a binding energy of approximately $36~{\rm{MeV}}$ below its four-meson threshold and propose searches in the $4μ$ and $4\mu2π$ final states.

titles.title: A toy model for hadronic bonds in exotic hadrons

abstracts.value: We formulate massless tree-level Compton scattering as an effective two-qubit operation on electron and photon helicities. In the Bell basis, the scattering map separates into two parity sectors and admits a simple quantum circuit representation with one nonunitary filter. After Kraus normalization, this filter defines an unsharp incomplete Bell measurement that distinguishes the two Bell-parity sectors but not the relative Bell label within each sector. We further show that the incomplete measurement alone does not surpass the classical teleportation threshold, whereas a subsequent complete Bell-basis readout enables unit conditional teleportation fidelity.

titles.title: Quantum circuit representation and incomplete Bell measurements in Compton scattering

abstracts.value: A subharmonic mixer topology is introduced that uses quarter-wave stubs to create virtual RF/LO grounds and provide impedance matching in close proximity to the antiparallel Schottky barrier diode pair, thereby reducing the electrical length and enabling broadband operation. The RF/LO matching topology is demonstrated at 600 GHz and 1200 GHz, with good agreement between measured and simulated performance. The 600-GHz mixer demonstrates approximately 20% RF bandwidth with a DSB receiver noise temperature below 1300 K across most of the measured band, while the 1200-GHz implementation achieves DSB receiver noise temperatures below 3000 K over a broad frequency range. Both mixers are characterized at room temperature with approximately 2 mW of LO power. The 600-GHz mixer is used in the Submillimeter Wave Instrument (SWI) onboard ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer. Overall, these results demonstrate state-of-the-art room-temperature performance for broadband receiver front ends targeting atmospheric research and remote-sensing applications.

titles.title: Broadband 600- and 1200-GHz Subharmonically Pumped Schottky Diode Mixers

abstracts.value: Sample-based quantum linear solvers measure quantum Krylov states $e^{-iAT}|b\rangle$ and reconstruct the solution of $Ax=b$ classically on the observed basis states. We develop this approach for positive-definite systems that arise from elliptic partial differential equations. We show that the sampling guarantees hold in any fixed basis with an efficient transform. We then replace the variational reconstruction by a Galerkin solve on the sampled set. For this reconstruction we derive expected and high-probability energy-norm error bounds, a sample complexity in terms of the smallest sampling probability on an essential set, a computable residual certificate, and a support-completeness theorem for the dephased outcome law. We formulate the method for elliptic problems on Riemannian cross sections. In two dimensions the stiffness matrix is metric-independent in conformal coordinates, and curved vessels lead to the same matrix class. Killing symmetries of the cross section give selection rules for the measurement outcomes, and the Lie derivative of the metric gives first-order bounds for geometric perturbations. We separate operator approximations, whose effect we bound, from sampler approximations, which affect coverage but not the target. As examples we treat the implicit step of pulsatile flow in elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts. In simulations of up to 12 qubits, the number of Fourier modes required for 1% error grows from 14 to 60 while the number of unknowns grows from 64 to 4096. A classical residual-greedy selection is nevertheless more efficient than quantum sampling in all cases studied, consistent with the low measured sampling efficiency. On a six-qubit trapped-ion processor, the measured outcome laws follow a replacement-noise model whose strength grows by about 0.6% per two-qubit gate, and a parity selection rule rejects shots at the predicted rate.

titles.title: Riemannian Formulation of Sample-Based Quantum Krylov Solvers for Elliptic Problems: Energy-Norm Guarantees and Duct-Flow Applications

abstracts.value: Fluorescence response matrix imaging enables separate computational correction of excitation and emission aberrations through dual deconvolution, but single-focus acquisition requires a large number of camera frames, limiting its practical use. Multifocal excitation can accelerate acquisition by recording many illumination positions in parallel, but denser foci also increase inter-focus crosstalk, which can bias the estimated excitation and emission optical transfer functions and degrade aberration correction. Here, we introduce high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging with adaptive multifocal illumination, in which the inter-focus spacing of the multifocal lattice is adjusted according to specimen-dependent crosstalk. A programmable digital micromirror device generates multifocal excitation lattices, and the resulting detector-resolved fluorescence responses are assembled into a two-coordinate fluorescence response matrix. Dual deconvolution separately estimates and corrects the excitation and emission optical transfer functions, and the aberration-corrected matrix is then combined in the spatial-frequency domain to reconstruct the aberration-free image. This strategy reduces the number of required camera frames by approximately three orders of magnitude, allowing response matrices with $\sim 10^6$ illumination positions to be acquired within seconds to a few minutes. The accelerated acquisition preserves the aberration-correction capability of dual deconvolution and achieves an estimated lateral resolution of $\sim$100 nm. Applied to heterogeneous mouse brain and kidney tissue, the method enables high-resolution, depth-resolved volumetric imaging while correcting specimen-dependent aberrations. Together, these results establish adaptive multifocal illumination as a practical route to high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging.

titles.title: Dual deconvolution multifocal fluorescence response matrix microscopy for aberration-free high-throughput super-resolution imaging

abstracts.value: The recent observation of an excess near the kinematic $t\bar{t}$ production threshold by the CMS and ATLAS collaborations suggests the existence of a color-singlet and $S$-wave quasi-bound state of top quark. Due to the non-relativistic nature of top and anti-top quarks in this threshold region, toponium production provides an ideal system to probe the anomalous dipole moments of the top quark. In this work, we investigate the impact of chromo-electric dipole moment (CEDM) in $t\bar{t}$-gluon vertex on toponium production at the LHC. We implement the enhanced near-threshold production of the spin-0 color-singlet toponium state $η_t$ via gluon fusion. The resonant toponium contribution is then combined with the continuum $t\bar{t}$ production amplitude, including the interference effects induced by the top CEDM. Furthermore, we construct a set of asymmetries based on the angular distributions of charged leptons in the leptonic decay channel of $t\bar{t}$. Finally, we derive the expected exclusion limit on the top quark CEDM parameter $d_t^g$ using these lepton angular asymmetries.

titles.title: Probing the chromo-electric dipole moment of top quark near the toponium production threshold at LHC

abstracts.value: In this paper, we study phase transitions and scalar quasinormal modes(QNMs) of magnetically charged Euler--Heisenberg-dilaton AdS black holes in the extended phase space. abstracts.value: We show that criticality concentrates extensive sensing information into a local trajectory. In the rapid-readout limit of an all-to-all dissipative feedback network, a single binary trajectory has a Fisher-information rate linear in $N$ for a common weak field, as does the full record. Critical slowing does not remove this gain because the local weight of the slow mode decreases with $N$. An analytic bound guarantees that the local record retains more than half of the full information across the entire channel-parameter range. We also identify how parameter drives and observation dynamics determine local access to collective information beyond permutation symmetry. Furthermore, our sparse-readout theorem establishes a $k^{-1}$ decay of fractional information loss: only $Θ(\varepsilon^{-1})$ trajectories are needed to retain a fraction $1-\varepsilon$ of the full information rate. Any growing readout set, even of vanishing density, asymptotically recovers the full common-field Fisher-information rate.

titles.title: Criticality Concentrates Extensive Sensing Information into a Local Readout

abstracts.value: We study dynamical chiral symmetry breaking in $(2{+}1)$-dimensional QED on a rigidly rotating disc, $ΩR<1$, within the rainbow Schwinger--Dyson framework. At zero temperature the rotation response of the condensate vanishes identically, so $N_c^{\rm SD}(Ω,T{=}0)=N_c^{\rm SD}(0)=2.60\pm0.01$ (using three operational definitions). At finite temperature, rotation suppresses the condensate through a dominant occupation-reweighting channel, $\hatκ_{\rm occ}=-1.55$, accounting for $\ge 99.995\%$ of the linearized total response at the reference parameters, with self-consistent feedback amplifying it by $26.5$. The screening channel is reported at fixed regularization, $\hatκ_{\rm scr}(\varepsilon = 0.01)=-0.97$; its $\varepsilon \to 0$ behavior is logarithmically divergent. The crossover flavor $N^{*}(Ω)$ falls monotonically at fixed temperature (a corollary). The critical flavor number is unchanged by rotation at $T=0$ (theorem). Together these results set the finite-temperature reference for the model.

abstracts.value: The Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan (GKLS) equation, a cornerstone of open-system theory, describes Markovian semigroup dynamics in which information about the initial preparation cannot revive. Beyond this regime, information revivals are widely interpreted as backflow from a non-Markovian environment. However, a decrease followed by an increase in information retrievable from the system need not imply that information has returned from the environment [PRX Quantum 6, 020316 (2025)]. It may instead arise from noise correlations unrelated to the system's initial preparation, carried by inert degrees of freedom that never interact with the system and therefore cannot mediate backflow. Such revivals are called extrinsic; genuine backflow is reserved for revivals that cannot be explained this way. The framework developed in that work, however, assumes access to arbitrary initial system states, an assumption often incompatible with physical constraints or limited experimental control. This leaves open which properties of the available preparations are necessary for an information revival to certify genuine backflow. Here we extend the framework to allow the description of restricted families of initial states and show that genuine backflow is possible only if the family contains noncommuting states. If all available states commute, as in a classical stochastic process, every revival can be explained by a suitable inert extension and is therefore extrinsic. Noncommutativity of the available system states is thus necessary for information revivals to provide an operational signature of environmental memory.

titles.title: Genuine Information Backflow Requires Noncommuting Initial System States

abstracts.value: We present a comprehensive broadband spectro-temporal analysis of the dynamically confirmed Galactic black hole transient GS 1354-64 during its 2025-26 outburst, using near-simultaneous observations from Insight-HXMT and XRISM. The high spectral resolution of the XRISM-Resolve microcalorimeter, coupled with the high-cadence broadband coverage of Insight-HXMT, reveals a dramatic evolution in the inner accretion geometry. During the early hard-intermediate state, the spectrum was dominated by a hot Comptonizing corona accompanied by relativistically broadened reflection features. As the outburst progressed, the corona cooled efficiently, the photon index steepened (Gamma >~ 2.5), and the reflection signatures, including the broad Fe K-alpha emission, were quenched, yielding a featureless, disk-dominated continuum. Concurrently, Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) evolved from 0.25 Hz to 6.52 Hz. Cross-spectral timing analysis revealed that the broadband X-ray time lags changed from pronounced positive (hard) delays (~160 ms) at low frequencies to near zero as the source softened. However, a statistical analysis incorporating the measurement uncertainties shows that the broadband lags lack a significant monotonic correlation with the QPO frequency, photon index, or fractional rms. Instead, the scattered lag behavior suggests a competition between positive Comptonization delays and negative thermal reverberation. While the spectral softening and QPO acceleration provide strong evidence for a geometric contraction of the corona (whether interpreted via Lense-Thirring precession or the Two-Component Advective Flow (TCAF) paradigm), the broadband timing properties underscore the turbulent and inhomogeneous nature of the inner flow as the advancing Keplerian disk drives the source into the soft state.

titles.title: Mapping the Contracting Corona in GS 1354-64 with Insight-HXMT and XRISM: Evolving X-ray Lags and Quenched Reflection across a Complete State Transition

abstracts.value: We formulate the finite-time response problem for a radially accelerated Unruh--DeWitt detector coupled to a real massless scalar field outside a static, spherically symmetric, horizonless compact star. The stellar exterior is described by the Schwarzschild geometry, while unresolved field--surface interactions are represented by a local Robin condition at the stellar radius. After reducing the Klein--Gordon equation to a half-line Schrödinger problem, we identify a sufficiently stable branch of the Robin family from positivity of the radial operator, construct delta-normalized continuum modes, and define the static ground state with respect to Schwarzschild time. We derive a mode-amplitude representation of the smoothly switched detector response that avoids a direct numerical treatment of the coincidence singularity of the Wightman distribution. We obtain a radially aligned trajectory of constant signed proper acceleration in terms of the rapidity measured by static observers. The resulting formulation separates the effects of compactness, surface condition, closest approach, detector gap, and interaction duration. We also state the flat-space, Dirichlet, static-detector, low-frequency, large-distance, and long-interaction limits required to validate a numerical implementation. The framework provides a controlled extension of detector studies with static reflective compact objects to finite-time moving probes.

titles.title: Boundary-induced corrections to the response of an Unruh-DeWitt detector outside a compact star with Robin surface conditions

abstracts.value: We present a unified Bayesian analysis of Higgs-portal, neutron-decay, and axion-like-particle (ALP)-mediated dark matter in neutron stars within the single-fluid approximation. Using a common relativistic mean-field description of hadronic matter, we combine finite-nucleus and heavy-ion collision data, chiral effective field theory, NICER measurements of four pulsars, and GW170817. The individual dark-sector parameters remain weakly determined, while model-dependent shifts in nuclear skewness reveal the sensitivity of the inferred hadronic equation of state to the assumed dark-matter mechanism. The three scenarios yield substantially overlapping mass-radius and tidal-deformability predictions, with median maximum masses near $2.1\,M_\odot$. For $1.4\,M_\odot$ stars, the Higgs-portal model predicts higher $f$-mode frequencies and shorter damping times than the neutron-decay and ALP models, although their credible regions overlap. Comparison with three consistently reanalysed two-fluid models gives the largest Bayesian evidence to neutron decay: under the adopted priors, its Bayes factors relative to the Higgs-portal and two-fluid alternatives are approximately $24$-$37$, but only $2.2$ relative to ALP. This ranking concerns complete dark-matter models and does not establish a general preference for either fluid description or evidence for a dark component itself. Improved nuclear constraints and future gravitational-wave asteroseismology could provide complementary information to disentangle the hadronic and dark-sector contributions.

titles.title: Bayesian exploration of weakly interacting models of dark matter admixed neutron stars based on multi-density constraints

abstracts.value: Using a data sample corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 43.8~fb$^{-1}$ collected with the \mbox{BESIII} detector at 44 center-of-mass energy points between 3.510 and 4.946~GeV, the Born cross sections for the process $e^+e^- \to p \bar{n} π^-$ and its charge-conjugated process are measured. abstracts.value: Computational research in physics requires continuous interplay between simulation and scientific interpretation, demanding substantial specialist effort. Here we introduce Brilliance, a research agent that combines large language models, reusable physics knowledge and numerical simulation to conduct adaptive investigations in accelerator physics. Given a single user prompt, Brilliance designs a fourth-generation synchrotron light source that meets coupled emittance and nonlinear-acceptance requirements. Further exploration yields a design combining sub-10-pm emittance with a large dynamic aperture under realistic engineering constraints, suggesting a route towards hard-X-ray diffraction-limited operation, although the momentum-acceptance target remains unmet. Brilliance also calibrates a model of an operating light source against measured responses, accurately inferring its lattice and calibration errors. Across these studies, Brilliance autonomously revises its computational strategies in response to numerical evidence. These results demonstrate a route towards delegating sustained scientific investigations to agents equipped with domain expertise and numerical tools.

titles.title: Brilliance: toward autonomous computational research in particle accelerator physics

abstracts.value: The local Hilbert space dimension is a fundamental parameter in quantum many-body systems, but its role in controlling the ergodicity-breaking transition remains less explored. We systematically study this question by introducing toy models of qudits in zero dimensions that exhibit an ergodicity-breaking transition. Using the hybridization condition, we analytically obtain the dependence of the critical value of the interactions on the local Hilbert space dimension. Numerical studies of spectral correlation measures show agreement with the theoretical predictions, hence confirming the existence of the ergodicity-breaking transition in these models. We further introduce a distinct higher spin version of the model and numerically obtain the same critical behavior, demonstrating that the observed critical point is independent of the microscopic structure of interactions considered.

titles.title: Ergodicity breaking transition beyond qubits

abstracts.value: A characteristic feature of topological field theories is the absence of local propagating degrees of freedom. In four-dimensional BF theory with cosmological term, we make this feature manifest by exactly reducing the finite non-Abelian shift symmetry. We do so by identifying a higher dressing field, a 1-form compensating the shift, allowing to build from first principles the composite shift-invariant field $\boldsymbol{B}=B-λ^{-1}F$. In terms of this dressed field, the dynamics becomes algebraic and sets $\boldsymbol{B}=0$, directly exposing the absence of local propagating degrees of freedom. This provides the first explicit instance of the higher-form Dressing Field Method.

titles.title: Higher Dressing and Shift-Invariance in 4D Topological BF Theory

abstracts.value: Using established probabilistic measurement-reversal theory, we study recovery placement in encoded-qutrit teleportation under monitored decay. We characterize the success advantage of reversing a no-jump map only on the encoded support and compare two receiver capabilities. The restricted-map construction applies to general finite-dimensional supports; explicit timing results are obtained for a coherent V-type sender, a $Λ$-type receiver, and $S=\{0,2\}$, within a prescribed family of maximal exact sender reversals. With one outcome-independent full-space receiver filter, we maximize success probability at fixed total time subject to a minimum success-weighted conditional fidelity. A single preassigned recovery time yields up to three duration-dependent regimes: no sender reversal, the earliest feasible intermediate reversal, and final-time reversal. If recovery times may be randomized independently of the input and only the pooled successful ensemble must meet the fidelity requirement, the optimum over all such timing distributions mixes the two endpoints for $ΓT \ge (\ln 3)/2$. With Bell-outcome-dependent nonunitary receiver recovery, each accepted full-column-rank transfer branch can instead be reversed exactly. For the same model and sender-operation family, omitting sender reversal uniquely maximizes the exact-teleportation success probability for every finite $T>0$ at positive decay rate. Partial pathway coherence further distinguishes relative support gain from absolute recovery success: the long-time dark-state plateau survives only for fully coherent decay. These results show how receiver control capabilities and the meaning of the fidelity constraint determine whether intermediate sender recovery is useful.

titles.title: Receiver-Constrained Recovery Placement for Encoded-Qutrit Teleportation under Monitored Decay

abstracts.value: The detection and quantification of quantum entanglement are central problems in quantum information science. Based on the realignment of density matrices and the vectorization of reduced density matrices, we construct a family of enhanced separability criteria for bipartite and multipartite quantum systems. Our criteria recover the previously proposed realignment-based criteria as special cases and detect more entanglement than the earlier ones. Moreover, we derive tighter lower bounds for the concurrence and the convex-roof extended negativity, criteria for detecting the genuine tripartite entanglement, and lower bounds on genuine-multipartite-entanglement concurrence. The advantages of our results are demonstrated with detailed examples.

titles.title: Separability criteria and lower bounds of entanglement via realignment

abstracts.value: Spatial interference can break the inversion symmetry of an effective Josephson potential even in a laterally homogeneous junction with inversion-symmetric local energy. We derive a general criterion based on harmonic-dependent complex spatial form factors: a single local harmonic remains a shifted cosine, whereas multiple harmonics can acquire phases incompatible with any common inversion center, permitting cubic interactions and three-wave mixing. Phase reflection reverses all odd-order expansion coefficients about corresponding minima while preserving the even-order ones. For a capacitively shunted junction at fixed charging energy and arbitrary offset charge, it also preserves the complete quantum spectrum, enabling reversal of the odd nonlinear sector without spectral retuning. A centered cross junction with multiple local harmonics is one concrete example. Within the imposed-field model, a three-component magnetic field can generate an inversion-asymmetric effective potential, and reversing an odd number of field components exactly reflects it without changing the quantum spectrum of the capacitively shunted junction.

titles.title: Spatial interference changes the symmetry class of a Josephson element

abstracts.value: The feasibility of real-time track fitting of straight tracks for online event selection is shown in the context of the MUonE experiment. In order to reach the high throughput and low latency required for real-time track fitting, the tracking algorithm is implemented using High-Level Synthesis for an FPGA, which provides provides a balance between flexibility and performance. Hardware tracking results from a test with high-rate muons at the CERN M2 beam are presented. This test, a joint effort by the MUonE and Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiments, operated with Two-Strip (2S) modules provided by the CMS tracker group. The prototype version of the fitter used in this test achieves 3.75 $μ$s latency and 7.75 % resource use. A comparison of the results with those obtained from a pure software implementation shows agreement well below relevant uncertainty scales. Developments since the test are also presented, with the hardware algorithm now reaching 1.35 $μ$s latency and producing pipelined fitting results above 50 MHz while requiring less resources than the initial version. Doing so required including certain assumptions in the algorithm, but these assumptions hold for linear track fitting in general and algorithm remains useful in contexts other than MUonE.

titles.title: Real-time Track Reconstruction with FPGAs: an example from MUonE
